[context] The moon too,
the companion of the sun, has many names, e.g. Soma, because she is lucky, and everything lucky is called somagraha, whilst all that is unlucky is called papagraha. Further, Nisesa, i.e. lord of the night, Nakshatranatha, i.e. lord of the lunar stations, Dvijesvara, i.e. lord of the Brahmins, Sitamsu, i.e. having a cold ray, because the moon's globe is watery, which is a blessing to the earth. When the solar ray meets the moon, the ray becomes as cool as the moon herself, then, being reflected, it illuminates the darkness, makes the night cool and extinguishes any hurtful kind of combustion wrought by the sun. Similarly the moon is also called Candra, which means the left eye of Narayana, as the sun is his right eye.

# وإنما جعلنا البعد

من عند نصف النهار لأن التعديل للميلاد به أسهل من العمل بالآفاق وساعات النهار
الأطول لعرض بيت المقدس أربع عشرة ساعة وشئ فلا يستقيم عمل اليهود
بالساعات الزمانية إلا أن يكون الاجتماع لرأس تشري واقعاً مع الاعتدال
الخريفي وليس يقع معه أبداً بل يتقدمه ويتأخر عنه مقداراً كثيراً كما بينا
فيما تقدم فإذا استخرجنا وقت الاجتماع بالحساب الذي أورده اليهود في الجدول
الذي حللناه على رأيهم ترقينا من ذلك إلى علم أول السنة ومعرفة كيفيتها
في النقصان والاعتدال والتمام وقد تقدمت لنا المعرفة بما هي بسيطة أم كبيسة
فنطلب في جدول الحدود مدة من أيام الأسبوع يتضمن حدّاها طرفاها الوقت
الذي خرج لنا الاجتماع فيه في جانب الكبوس إن كانت كبوساً وفي جانب البسائط إن
كانت بسيطة فإذا وجدناه ألفينا بحذائه أول السنة من الأسبوع وكيفيتها
وإذا علمنا أول السنة وكيفيتها وركبنا تلك الكيفية مع البساطة
أو الكبوس عرفنا من ذلك مضي أول السنة المقبلة

(In this our calculation of the conjunction) we have used noon as terminus a quo for no other reason but this, that we may more easily find the equation for the moled by this method than by using the horizons (i.e. reckoning from sunset, as the Jews do).
The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem are 13h. plus a fraction. Therefore the calculation of the Jews by ὧραι καιρικαί is incorrect, except in case the conjunction at the beginning of Tishri should coincide with the autumnal equinox. This, however, never happens. On the contrary, the conjunction at the beginning of Tishri always either precedes or follows the autumnal equinox by a considerable space of time, as we have explained heretofore.
Relation between the beginning of the Year and its Character. — If we, now, make out the time of the conjunction by the traditional calculation of the Jews, or by means of the table which we have constructed according to their theory, we arrive at the knowledge of the beginning of the year and of its character, whether it be imperfect, intermediate, or perfect, whilst we have already previously learnt how to know whether the year be a common or a leap year. Thereupon we look in the Table of Limits for a space of time in the week within the limits of which the conjunction as found by our calculation falls. If the year be a leap year, we look into the column of leap years; if it be a common year, we look into the column of common years. Having made out this, we find opposite the indication of the week-day on which the year commences, and of the quality of the year. Once knowing the beginning of the year (its precise date in the week) and its quality, and combining with it our knowledge as to whether the year is a common or a leap year, we come to know the beginning of the next following year.
Here follows the Table of the Limits:—

# We have set the distance

from the meridian <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> because adjusting for a birth is easier by this method than by working with horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and some fraction. Therefore, the Jewish method using seasonal hours <note>original: "al-sa'at al-zamaniyya"; hours that vary in length based on the season</note> is not accurate unless the conjunction <note>original: "al-ihtima'"; the new moon</note> for the beginning of the month of Tishrei occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. This never actually happens. Rather, it precedes or follows the equinox by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their views, we then proceed to determine the start of the year and its quality in terms of being deficient, regular, or complete. We have already established whether the year is a common year <note>original: "basita"; a twelve-month year</note> or a leap year <note>original: "kabisa"; a thirteen-month year</note>. We then search the Table of Limits for a duration of weekdays whose boundaries include the time we found for the conjunction. We look in the leap year section if it is a leap year, and in the common year section if it is a common year. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the week for the start of the year and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as common or leap, we can determine the arrival of the following year's start.

# This is the Table of Limits

# The Reason We Set the Distance

We have set the distance from the point of midday <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"; the local meridian</note> because the <term>rectification</term> <gloss>adjustment of a planetary position or time</gloss> for a birth is easier with it than working with local horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish method of calculation using <term>seasonal hours</term> <gloss>unequal hours that vary in length depending on the time of year</gloss> is not accurate unless the <term>conjunction</term> <gloss>the moment of the new moon</gloss> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. This never happens consistently; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their system, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the beginning of the year and the determination of its quality—whether it is <term>deficient</term> <gloss>has fewer days than standard</gloss>, <term>regular</term> <gloss>standard length</gloss>, or <term>complete</term> <gloss>has additional days</gloss>. We already know whether the year is <term>simple</term> <gloss>common year</gloss> or <term>intercalary</term> <gloss>leap year</gloss>. We then search the Table of Limits for a duration of weekdays whose boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the section for intercalary years if it is a leap year, or the section for simple years if it is a common year. When we find it, we find alongside it the weekday for the start of the year and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as simple or intercalary, we can determine the beginning of the following year.

"At the time of rein-twisting (assaulting) — for a king
"It is not proper to conquer by stealth."
Another spy began,
Saying: — "Dara prepared not such an army
"That, in the imagination, could compute it
"Those persons (officers) who are army-understanding."
Sikandar said to him: — "A sharp sword
"Makes shreds of the hide of a hundred oxen."
To the army, such an excellent reply,
From the lofty monarch, was agreeable.
Every moment, news became more ardent (instant),
That the raging dragon (Dara) had come.
When Sikandar knew that that fierce cloud
Brought forth, thunder-like, the sword's flash (of battle),
He sent (a messenger), — that an army, from every region,
Should set out to the monarch's door.
From Egypt, and Afranchiya, and Rum, and Russia,
An army, bride-like, became arrayed.
When that countless army became massed,
He sought the enumeration of the names of the renowned ones.
The general gave information that six hundred thousand
Warriors, extraordinary horsemen, were mustered.
When the business (mustering) of the army became completed,
He prepared an assembly (muster) — without wine-cup or music.
The brains (sages) of Rum sate attentive;
They made the wax (of the heart) soft, in love for the king.
Of Dara's action (in invading his kingdom) and of his strife, — the king
Urged speech, and was perturbed as to his (Dara's) action.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Alexander the Great's preparations for war against Darius III.</meta>

# 161

For a king, at the moment of turning the reigns <note>turning the horse's head toward battle</note>
Victory cannot be attained through stealth.
Another investigator began to report,
That Darius has prepared so much wealth <note>referring to the size and provisions of his army</note>,
That those who are experts in counting armies,
Could only estimate it through calculation.
Alexander said to him: "A single sharp blade
Can cut the fat of a hundred oxen into tiny pieces." <note>original: "yek tigh-e tiz... peyh-e sad gāvrā riz riz"</note> <margin>A sharp sword can cut through the thickest hide or the largest number of fat oxen; a metaphor for quality overcoming quantity.</margin>
That valuable answer to the troops
Came grandly from the grand monarch.
The news grew more urgent every moment
That a roaring dragon <note>referring to Darius</note> was approaching Rome <note>here used to mean Alexander’s Byzantine/Greek territories</note>.
When Alexander realized that fierce cloud <note>the approaching army</note>
Was flashing the lightning of its blades from afar,
He sent word so that armies from every land
Should set out toward the monarch's gate.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a massive throng,
He requested the count from the recorders of famous names.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand
Courageous, elite cavalrymen had emerged. <note>original: "mofrad savār" refers to specialized or champion warriors who fight alone.</note>
When the organization of the army was complete,
He held an assembly outside with wine and cups.
The wise minds of Rome sat together;
They softened their hearts like wax toward the King's seal. <note>They became fully obedient to Alexander's command.</note>
The King spoke of the affairs of Darius,
Discussing his deeds and his intentions.

<column-break/>

<note>The following sections translate the Persian footnotes provided in the original manuscript transcription.</note>

1. This means a single sword can shred the fat and grease of a hundred fattened oxen. Alternative readings in other manuscripts suggest: "Can pierce the hides of a hundred oxen" or "the backs of a hundred oxen."

2. This means that when Alexander realized Darius was like a violent cloud, drawing the lightning of his sword toward him with the roar of thunder.

3. This means the presenter and army-scribe reported that three hundred thousand unique cavalrymen had gathered. <term>Mofrad savār</term> <gloss>single rider</gloss> and <term>yekeh savār</term> <gloss>lone rider</gloss> refer to peerless and incomparable heroes. Some manuscript versions record the number as six hundred thousand.

4. This means that by the seal of Alexander's command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his orders. Soft wax accepts an impression more readily than hard wax.

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to reports of Darius's massive army with a metaphor about a sharp blade's power. He summons a global coalition of three hundred thousand elite soldiers and consults with his Roman advisors.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander the Great, Darius, military muster, cavalry, Rome, Egypt, Russia, Sharafnama, Nizami Ganjavi</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Alexander is preparing his response to the challenge posed by Darius.</meta>

For the King, at the time of turning the reins,
Victory cannot be found through theft.
Another investigator began to speak,
Saying that Darius has prepared such a vast force,
That one can only count it by estimation,
According to those who are experts in armies.
Alexander said to him: "A single sharp blade <note>original: "tigh-e tiz"</note>
Can cut the fat of a hundred oxen into small pieces." <note>A metaphor suggesting that a single superior force can dismantle a much larger, softer mass. The commentary notes variations: "cut the hide of a hundred oxen" or "the backs of a hundred oxen."</note>
Such a noble answer to the army
Came from the exalted Sovereign.
The news became more intense at every moment,
That a roaring dragon was coming toward Rome.
When Alexander realized that that fierce cloud <note>Darius is compared to a storm cloud flashing with the lightning of swords.</note>
Was rarely drawing the lightning of the blade,
He sent word so that the army from every land
Should set out toward the door of the Sovereign.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia <note>original: "Rus"</note>,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a massive crowd,
He requested a count of the names of the illustrious men.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand <note>A variant reading suggests six hundred thousand.</note>
Independent brave cavalrymen had emerged.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held a gathering outside with the goblet.
The wise minds of Rome sat together,
Softening the wax of their hearts with the King’s seal. <note>An idiom meaning they became fully submissive and obedient to his command, as soft wax receives an impression.</note>
The King spoke of the affairs of Darius,
Discussing his deeds and becoming preoccupied with his case.

<column-break/>

<summary>Alexander dismisses the numerical superiority of Darius with a metaphor about a sharp blade and gathers a massive international coalition of three hundred thousand troops.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander the Great, Darius, military mobilization, Rome, Egypt, Russia, Africa, Sharafnama, Nizami Ganjavi</keywords>

The king, at the time of turning the reins, said:
One cannot find victory through theft.
Another researcher began to say
That Darius has prepared so much fat
That it can be counted by estimation
By those who are experts of the army.
Alexander said to him: A single sharp sword
Cuts the fat of a hundred oxen into tiny pieces.
Such a precious answer to the army
Came forth from the exalted sovereign.
The news became hotter every moment
That a breathing dragon had come toward Rome.
When Alexander knew that that fierce cloud
Was rarely drawing the lightning of the sword,
He sent word so that the army from every region
Should set out toward the gate of the sovereign.
From Egypt, Africa, Rome, and Russia,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a multitude,
He requested the count of the names of the illustrious men.
The muster-master reported that three hundred thousand
Brave, single riders had come forward.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held a gathering outside with the cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat down;
They softened wax with the seal of the king.
The king spoke of the affair of Darius
And reflected upon his business.

<column-break/>

<margin>1. Meaning one sword cuts the fat and tallow of a hundred fattened oxen into tiny pieces. Variant: It cuts the hide of a hundred oxen, or the backs of a hundred oxen.</margin>
<margin>2. Meaning when Alexander knew that Darius was a fierce cloud that draws the lightning of the sword toward him with the roar of thunder.</margin>
<margin>3. Meaning the presenter and army-scribe reported that three hundred thousand single riders were gathered. A single rider is a peerless hero. Variant: six hundred thousand.</margin>
<margin>4. Meaning they softened the wax of their hearts with the seal of Alexander's command and became accepting of his order. Soft wax accepts a seal sooner than hard wax.</margin>

<summary>Alexander the Great responds to reports of Darius’s massive army by asserting that a single sharp sword can overcome a vast force. He mobilizes his own diverse military coalition from across his empire in preparation for the coming conflict with the Persian king.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander the Great, Darius, military mobilization, Rome, Egypt, Russia, Africa, chivalry, sword imagery</keywords>

[context] My heart was grieved at his miserable plight, (and) I thought it inhuman, in such a state, to irritate the poor man's wound
with reproach, and sprinkle salt thereon; I said to myself,—
Distichs.
The wretched fellow, in the extreme of intoxication,
Was not apprehensive of the day of distress.
A tree drops its blossoms and fruit profusely in spring;
In winter, as a matter of course, it remains leafless.
STORY VI.
A king made his son over to a teacher, and said, "He is thy son; educate him in the same way as a son of thine own." He replied, "I am your obedient servant." For some years he laboured hard, and exerted himself in his behoof, (but) he made no progress, while the teacher's own sons became perfect in scholarship and rhetoric. The king took the learned man to task, and censured him, saying, "Thou hast acted contrary to thy promise, and hast not fulfilled the conditions of fidelity." He replied, "It cannot be concealed from the world-adorning judgment of the lord of the earth, that education is the same, but capacities differ."
Stanza.
Although silver and gold come out of stone,
There is not silver and gold in every stone.

Accepting blame and pouring salt on the wound: I did not see the wisdom in this. I said to myself:

**Poetic Fragment**
The companion at the table should not become drunk
at the end of the feast.
The day the locust reaches its hand into the trees in springtime,
The crime is that the trees remain without leaves in winter.

**Parable**
A king entrusted his son to a <term>tutor</term> <gloss>an educator and man of letters</gloss>, saying: "Nurture my child just as you would one of your own children." The tutor labored for several years, and the result was that the tutor's own children reached the pinnacle of knowledge, yet the king's son remained ignorant. The king summoned the wise man and rebuked him, saying: "You have broken your promise and failed to fulfill the conditions of our agreement." 

The tutor replied: "O Lord of the Earth, let it not remain hidden from your enlightened mind that although the education is the same, the inherent nature is different."

**Poetic Fragment**
Although silver and gold come out of stone,
They are not found in every stone.

<summary>A tutor explains to a king that while education can be applied equally to all, the inherent character and potential of the student determine the ultimate outcome. This page explores the tension between nurture and nature through the metaphor of minerals found only in specific stones.</summary>
<keywords>Sa'di, Gulistan, education, nature vs nurture, kingship, wisdom, Persian literature</keywords>

Enduring blame and pouring salt on the wound <note>an idiom for adding insult to injury</note>. I did not see the benefit in it. I said to myself:

**Poem** <note>original: "qit'ah", a specific poetic form</note>
A companion at the table should not become drunk at the end.
Locusts strip the trees of their gold <note>referring to leaves</note> in a single day.
If the trees scatter their leaves in the spring,
They will remain branchless and bare in the winter.

**Story**
A king entrusted his son to a <term>tutor</term> <gloss>adib</gloss> and said, "Nurture my child just as you would one of your own children." The tutor labored for several years and achieved results, but while his own children became highly accomplished in knowledge, the prince remained ignorant. The king summoned the scholar, reprimanding and rebuking him. He said, "You have broken your promise and did not fulfill the conditions of our agreement." The tutor replied: 

"O Sovereign of the Earth, let it not remain hidden from your luminous mind that while the education is the same, natures differ."

**Poem**
Though silver and gold come out of stone,
They are not to be found in every stone.

<summary>A tutor explains to a king that education cannot overcome a student's inherent nature, using the analogy of precious metals found only in specific stones. The page also includes a brief reflection on the folly of wasting resources prematurely.</summary>
<keywords>education, inherent nature, king and tutor, Sa'di, Gulistan, morality, character</keywords>

When, on account of asininity, a tethered ass becomes violent, both his (fore-)legs will be shackled in addition.
Then the ass will say, “One tether is enough for me”; (but) in sooth do not think (that such is the case), for those two are (result) from the action of that vile creature.
In exposition of the following Hadith of Mustafa (Mohammed), on whom be peace: “Verily, the most High God created the angels and set reason in them, and He created the beasts and set lust in them, and He created the sons of Adam and set in them reason and lust; and he whose reason prevails over his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust prevails over his reason is lower than the beasts.”
It is related in the Hadith that the majestical God created the creatures of the world (in) three kinds.
One class (He made) entirely reason and knowledge and munificence; that is the angel: he knoweth naught but prostration in worship.
In his original nature is no concupiscence and sensuality: he is absolute light, (he is) living through (his) love of God.
Another class is devoid of knowledge, like the animal (which lives) in fatness from (eating) fodder.
It sees nothing but stable and fodder: it is heedless of (future) misery and glory (felicity).
The third (class) is Adam’s descendant and Man: half of him is of the angel and half of him is ass.
The ass-half, indeed, inclines to that which is low; the other half inclines to that which is rational.
Those two classes (the angels and the beasts) are at rest from war and combat, while this Man is (engaged) in torment (painful struggle) with two adversaries.
And, moreover, this (race of) Man, through probation, has been divided: they (all) are of human shape, but (in truth) they have become three communities (families).
One party have become submerged absolutely and, like Jesus, have attained unto the (nature of the) angel.
The form (of such a one is that of) Adam, but the reality is Gabriel: he has been delivered from anger and sensual passion and (vain) disputation.
He has been delivered from discipline and asceticism and self-mortification: you would say he was not even born of a child of Adam.
The second sort have attained unto (the nature of) asses: they have become pure anger and absolute lust.
The qualities of Gabriel were in them and departed: that house was (too) narrow, and those qualities (too) grand.
The person who is deprived of (the vital) spirit becomes dead: when his spirit is deprived of those (angelic qualities), he becomes an ass,
Because the spirit that hath not those (qualities) is vile: this word is true, and the (perfect) Sufi has said (it).
He (the man of animal nature) suffers more anxiety than the beasts, (for) he practises subtle arts in the world.
The cunning and imposture which he knows how to spin — that (cunning) is not produced by any other animal.
To weave gold-embroidered robes, to win pearls from the bottom of the sea.
The fine artifices of geometry or astronomy, and the science of medicine and philosophy —
Which are connected only with this world and have no way (of mounting) up to the Seventh Heaven —
All this is the science of building the (worldly) stable which is the pillar (basis) of the existence of (persons like) the ox and the camel.
For the sake of preserving the animal for a few days, these crazy fools have given to those (arts and sciences) the name of “mysteries.”

<summary>This page explains a Prophetic tradition categorizing beings into three types: angels (pure intellect), animals (pure lust), and humans (a mixture of both). Rumi describes how humans can transcend to an angelic state or fall below the level of beasts depending on whether intellect or lust dominates.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Lust, Angels, Beasts, Humanity, Gabriel, Hadith, Philosophy, Asceticism</keywords>

Like a donkey with its feet tied, stubborn and foolish,
he tied both his feet and then upon his head
like a blindfolded donkey he bolted.
Then the donkey says, one bond is enough for me,
indeed that is the act of a lowly person.
Truly, for a donkey, one bond is enough for the head.

### In explanation of that tradition of the Chosen One <note>The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him</note>: "Verily, God the Exalted created the angels and placed within them intellect; and He created the beasts and placed within them lust; and He created the children of Adam and placed within them both intellect and lust. Thus, he whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth.

It has come in the tradition that the Glorious Lord,
The Creator of the world, created three kinds of beings.
One group possesses only intellect, knowledge, and generosity,
that is the angel; he knows nothing but prostration.
There is no greed or desire in his fundamental nature,
he is pure light, living through the love of God.
Another group is entirely void of knowledge,
like the animal, thriving on fodder.
He perceives nothing except the stable and the feed,
he is ignorant of wretchedness and of honor.
The third kind is the son of Adam, the human being,
one half of him is inclined toward the sublime.
The other half is like a donkey, inclined toward the base,
and this human is made of wind and contradiction.
Those two groups <note>angels and animals</note> are at peace from war and strife,
while humans are tested and divided into three communities.
One group has become entirely submerged <note>in the Divine</note>,
like Jesus, they have joined with the angels.
They are delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk,
they have the form of a man but the meaning of Gabriel.
They are released from self-discipline, asceticism, and struggle,
they have arrived from humanity and their own lineage.
Another group has joined with the beasts,
they have become pure anger and absolute lust.
The house <note>the body</note> was too narrow for that lofty description,
the angelic quality in them has faded away.
The person becomes like a corpse, one who is soulless,
because the soul that does not have the Beloved is lowly.
He makes his soul even lower than the animals,
through the craftiness and deception he knows how to weave.
He knows how to weave gold-embroidered garments,
and how to find pearls at the bottom of the sea.
With astronomy, the science of medicine, and philosophy,
yet he has no path to the seventh heaven.
All this worldly attachment is focused on the stable,
the goal is only the preservation of the animal for a few days.
The fools have given these things the name of "universal mysteries."

<column-break/>

He made the creatures visible in three categories:
Those who are angels, engaged in prostration,
they became the manifestations of the love of God.
The animalistic group became bound by their nature,
they are heedless, wretched, and without honor.
The human race became capable of both good and evil,
the second half, like an angel, is noble-born.
The human is in a state of reaction between two opposites,
human in form, yet divided into three nations.
Truly, the company of the angelic station
is delivered from anger, lust, and empty talk.
You would say they are not born of Adam;
the last group is of the character of beasts.
Pure anger and absolute lust are found there,
the narrow house of the body has lost its high quality.
The soul becomes wretched when it is without the Beloved,
this speech is the word of God, keep it as an ornament for your hand.
He performs every meticulous task in the world,
tasks no other animal could perform.
Drawing jewels from the depths of the sea,
knowledge of philosophy, medicine, and astronomy.
But he has no passage to the seventh heaven,
he only pays attention to the ox and the camel.
He has named those follies "mysteries."

<summary>This page explains a Prophetic tradition regarding the three types of creation: angels (pure intellect), animals (pure lust), and humans (a mixture of both). Rumi describes the spiritual struggle of humanity to transcend animalistic needs and achieve an angelic state.</summary>
<keywords>intellect, lust, angels, animals, humanity, Jesus, Gabriel, spiritual struggle, philosophy, worldly knowledge</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Like a donkey whose legs are tied tightly because of its stubbornness,
He tied both its legs and placed it at the head.
When the muzzled donkey pulled its head and [bolted],
The donkey then said: "One binding is enough for me."
Indeed, the sewing of the donkey-hide is the act of that base one.
The donkey's mirror is tied with a single stitch.

### Concerning the commentary on the Hadith of the Chosen One, peace be upon him: "Indeed, God Almighty created the angels..."
"Indeed, God Almighty created the angels and endowed them with intellect; He created the beasts and endowed them with lust; and He created the children of Adam and endowed them with both intellect and lust. Thus, he whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Messenger of God spoke the truth.

He bound his own two feet with his own hands;
The act of the self is in that [field] and base.
This interprets the noble Hadith.

It came in the Hadith that the Glorious Lord,
The Creator of the world, created three kinds [of beings].
One class is of predominant intellect, knowledge, and generosity:
That is the angel; he knows nothing but prostration.
There is no greed or desire in his element;
He is absolute light, living by the love of God.
Another group is devoid of knowledge,
Like an animal [living] for fodder in the meadow.
He perceives nothing except the stable and fodder;
He is ignorant of wretchedness and of honor.
This third kind is the son of Adam, the human.
The other half is inclined toward the sublime.
Half is donkey, inclined toward the lowly;
And this human is composed of wind and opposition.
Those two groups are at rest from war and strife,
While humans are tested and became three communities.
And this human is divided by trial.
One group has become absolutely submerged,
Joined with the angels like Jesus.
Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk;
The form of man, but the meaning of Gabriel.
Delivered from asceticism, piety, and struggle;
As if they were not born of man.
Another group joined with the [beasts];
They became pure anger and absolute lust.
That house was narrow and that description [faded];
The Gabriel-like quality in them was [lost].
He made him dead, for the person who is without soul
Is lower than the animals, for he possesses no soul.
Because the soul that does not have [the Beloved] is base;
He lives a life lower than the beasts.
The deception and hypocrisy that he knows how to weave,
The weaving of gold-embroidered robes,
The finding of pearls in the depths of the sea;
With astronomy, the science of medicine, and philosophy—
These are all entirely related to this world.
He has no way to the seventh heaven.
Which was the pillar that the ox held?
They named those the "Mysteries of the Universe,"
Yet the purpose is the survival of the animal for a few days.

<keywords>Hadith, intellect, lust, angels, animals, Jesus, Gabriel, philosophy, medicine, spiritual ranks</keywords>

The physician should, after the same manner, cause to be prepared boluses and juices of other kinds of clean meat.

The administration of these promotes the supply of semen in one's body. 13

APHRODISIAC MEAT-JUICE OF BUFFELO.

Take a quantity of the seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus).

Drench them in water till sprouts come forth.

These should be carefully separated from other articles that may have been mixed with them;

The seeds, thus separated, should be husked.

With them should be mixed a quantity of the seeds (of the same measure) of Mucuna pruriens.

They should then be thrown into meat-juice made of buffalo-flesh, that has been enriched with ghee and dressed with curds and the juice of pomegranates.

Into it should then be thrown coriander seeds, cumin seeds, and dry ginger, each of proper measure;

By eating and drinking this preparation, one obtains an abundant supply of semen. 14-15

APHRODISIAC FISH AND FLESH.

He who eats fresh fish and flesh, as also Saphari, fried in ghee, obtains an inexhaustible supply of semen. 16

CONCEPTION-INDUCING PREPARATION.

One desirous of progeny should eat 'Rohita' fish fried in ghee and boiled in such meat-juice of goat's flesh as has been dressed with the juice of fruits, and then drink the remnant (that is left in the pot) of the meat-juice itself.

TWO PREPARATIONS OF CAKE HAVING APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some fish and fowl, and cut them into pieces.

Pound these pieces with assafoedita, 'Saindhava' salt, and corriander seeds.

Add wheat flour.

Make cakes of the product, with the aid of ghee. 18

Take some fish, and cut them into pieces.

Mix with them ghee, the expressed juice of pomegranates and other fruits of the same kind, and salt.

Boil the pieces, thus mixed, in the meat-juice of buffalo flesh.

When the meat-juice enters the fish, the fish should then be pounded. (The bones should all be extracted.)

To the pounded fish should then be added pepper, cumin seeds, corriander seeds, a little assafoedita, and new ghee.

The paste that results should be used as core or kernel of cakes made of the seeds of Phaseolus radiatus. 19-20

These two preparations of cakes possess nutritive virtues. They increase one's strength. They promote cheerfulness and bring good-luck.

Capable of increasing the semen, these prove beneficial in the matter of the birth of progeny. 21

MASHA CAKES OF APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus), Atmagupta (Mucuna pruriens), wheat-flour, 'Sali' rice, and 'Shastika' rice, and reduce them into a paste.

<meta>The text continues the section on aphrodisiac treatments and dietary preparations for vitality from the previous page of the Charaka Samhita.</meta>

### Chapter on Aphrodisiacs

Take clean sprouted black gram <term>masha</term> <gloss>Vigna mungo</gloss>, sweet fruits of the wood-apple <term>kapittha</term> <gloss>Limonia acidissima</gloss>, and place them in a large quantity of buffalo meat juice. This should be prepared with yogurt and pomegranate, and seasoned with coriander, cumin, and dry ginger. When this savory juice is drunk or eaten with a meal, it makes the semen inexhaustible.
-> Thus ends the recipe for buffalo juice aphrodisiac. <-

One who eats fresh fish or small fried <term>shaphari</term> <gloss>a species of small carp, Puntius sophore</gloss> in hot clarified butter <term>ghrita</term> will not suffer from exhaustion during sexual union with women.
-> Thus ends the recipe for fish fried in clarified butter as an aphrodisiac. <-

One who desires offspring should use <term>rohita</term> fish <gloss>Labeo rohita</gloss> fried in clarified butter and cooked in goat meat juice prepared with sour fruits. The fish should be eaten followed by the remaining juice.
-> Thus ends the formulation for promoting conception. <-

Prepare a mince of fish meat seasoned with asafoetida, rock salt, and coriander. Mix this with wheat flour and cook as small cakes <term>pupalika</term> <gloss>pancakes or fritters</gloss> in clarified butter. Alternatively, cook fish in buffalo meat juice that is rich in fat, sour, and salty. Once the juice is absorbed, crush the fish and add black pepper, cumin, coriander, a little asafoetida, and fresh clarified butter. This mixture should be used as a stuffing for cakes made of black gram flour. These two formulations for cakes are aphrodisiacs, strength-givers, and bestowers of excitement and good fortune. They provide nourishment and are excellent for increasing semen.
-> Thus ends the two formulations for aphrodisiac cakes. <-

A wise man having a regard for his reputation should not think of seducing a woman who is apprehensive, timid, not to be trusted, well guarded, or possessed of a father-in-law, or mother-in-law.

CHAPTER III.

EXAMINATION OF THE STATE OF A WOMAN'S MIND.

When a man is trying to gain over a woman he should examine the state of her mind, and acts as follows.

If she listens to him, but does not manifest to him in any way her own intentions, he should then try to gain her over by means of a go-between.

If she meets him once, and again comes to meet him better dressed than before, or comes to him in some lonely place, he should be certain that she is capable of being enjoyed by the use of a little force. A woman who lets a man make up to her, but does not give herself up, even after a long time, should be considered as a trifler in love, but owing to the fickleness of the human mind, even such a woman can be conquered by always keeping up a close acquaintance with her.

reference_meta.style_note: Victorian paraphrase that merges and reorders sūtras; sense is close but not a sūtra-by-sūtra crib
reference_meta.located: Book V (Pāradārika), ch. 2 closing verse 27 and colophon; ch. 3 (Bhāvaparīkṣā) sūtras 1-3 and the opening of sūtra 4
reference_meta.coverage_note: Reference covers the root text only; the Jayamaṅgalā commentary and the two colophons have no reference. Burton renders freely: verse 27 is folded into the prose paragraph ending ch. II; sūtra 1 = 'When a man is trying ... acts as follows'; sūtra 2 = 'If she listens to him ... go-between'; sūtra 3 (rejects the approach yet meets him again: of two minds, win her gradually) has no clean separate rendering; 'If she meets him once ... better dressed' corresponds to sūtra 4, which the page only begins. The final sentence ('A woman who lets a man make up to her ...') is either Burton's loose rendering of sūtra 3 or the following sūtra; it is kept as the boundary.

66. Example (the root and a fraction both subtracted). Of a flock of geese, ten times the square-root of the number departed for the Mánasa lake, on the approach of a cloud: an eighth part went to a forest of St'halapadminis: three couples were seen engaged in sport, on the water abounding with delicate fibres of the lotus. Tell, dear girl, the whole number of the flock.

Statement: Coeff. 10. Fraction [fraction illegible in OCR]. Given 6.

By the [second] rule (§ 63); unity, less the numerator of the fraction, is [fraction illegible in OCR]; and the coefficient and given number, being both divided by that, become [fraction illegible in OCR] and [fraction illegible in OCR]; and the half coefficient is [fraction illegible in OCR]. With these, proceeding by the [first] rule (§ 62), the number of the flock is found 144.

# Example
# Another Example

> When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew away to Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-growing lotuses. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in the water filled with tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word Order and Connection:** O young girl! Upon the arrival of the rainy season, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Manasa. An eighth part flew from the shore and went to a forest of land-growing lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in play in water adorned with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** O my dear one, sixteen years of age! There was a flock of swans. When the monsoon arrived, ten times the square root of their number went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of them flew from the edge of the water into a grove of land-growing lotuses <note>the *sthala-padmini* is a hibiscus variety that resembles a lotus</note>. Three pairs of swans, which equals 6 birds, were seen playing very lovingly in water beautiful with soft lotus fibers. Tell me, how many swans were in that flock? 3

**Mathematical Setup:** The multiplier of the square root <term>mulaguna</term> is 10. The fraction <term>ashtamsha</term> <gloss>1/8</gloss>. The visible remainder <term>drishyam</term> <gloss>6</gloss>. As per the rule stated previously for subtracting or adding fractions, we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by 1 minus the fraction <note>1 minus 1/8 equals 7/8</note>. Dividing by this fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss> results in: Visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>; Multiplier of the root <gloss>80/7</gloss>; Half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss>; The square of this half <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding the visible quantity gives <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result gives the flock of swans: 144.

**Expansion:** Following the rule mentioned in the second verse, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one. Thus, <gloss>1/1 minus 1/8</gloss> equals <gloss>7/8</gloss>. We divide the visible quantity 6 by this. <gloss>6/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> equals <gloss>6/1 multiplied by 8/7</gloss>, which is <gloss>48/7</gloss>. This becomes our adjusted visible quantity. Similarly, we divide the square root multiplier 10 by the same fraction. <gloss>10/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> equals <gloss>10/1 multiplied by 8/7</gloss>, which is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. This is our adjusted root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible amount and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the root multiplier, we perform the operation according to the method in the previous verse. That is, half of the root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Squaring this gives <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. This is then added to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<meta>The text breaks off as it begins the final addition to solve the quadratic equation. The previous page likely contained the general rule for equations involving square roots of the unknown.</meta>

# Example
# And another example

> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the monsoon season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew from the water’s edge toward a forest of land-growing lotuses. Oh young girl, three pairs of swans were seen sporting lovingly in the water, which was beautiful with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word-by-word connection:** Oh girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part flew from the shore of the water and reached a land-lotus forest. And three pairs of swans were seen engaged in play in the water adorned with young lotus roots. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** Oh beloved, who is sixteen years of age! There was a flock of swans. From that flock, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>of the total population</note> went away to Lake Manasa. One eighth part of the flock flew from the water's edge into a forest of land-lotuses. Three pairs of swans <note>totaling six birds</note> were seen playing with great affection in water made beautiful by tender lotus stalks. Say then, how many swans were in that flock? 3

**Statement of the problem:** Square root multiplier: 10; eighth part: <gloss>1/8</gloss>; visible amount: <gloss>6</gloss>. As it was stated <note>in the previous rule</note> that the quantity is decreased by the fractions, here the visible amount and the square root multiplier are divided by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible amount is <gloss>48/7</gloss> and the square root multiplier is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of this multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Its square <gloss>1600/49</gloss> added to the product of the visible amount results in <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Added to half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and then squared, the total flock of swans is found: 144.

**Elaboration:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one <note>the whole</note>, thus <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The visible quantity of 6 was divided by this, so <gloss>6/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. In this way, after performing the conversion by seven, <gloss>48/7</gloss> became the visible quantity <term>drishya rashi</term> <gloss>the known constant in the equation</gloss>. Similarly, the square root multiplier of 10 was divided by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, which is <gloss>10/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. After the conversion by seven, <gloss>80/7</gloss> became the root-multiplier quantity. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the square root multiplier, the calculation was performed according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is: half of the root multiplier became <gloss>40/7</gloss>. This was squared to become <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. This was then added to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is found: 144. ||

Thus, by giving the denominator of 7, <gloss>80/7</gloss> became the square root quantity. Ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Sloth and lack of initiative are a roadblock for wealth. Lack of adornment and decoration are a roadblock for beauty. Unsuitable activity is a roadblock for health. Bad friendship is a roadblock for ethical conduct. Lack of sense restraint is a roadblock for the spiritual life. Dishonesty is a roadblock for friends. Not rehearsing is a roadblock for learning. Not wanting to listen and ask questions are roadblocks for wisdom. Lack of commitment and reviewing are roadblocks for good qualities. Wrong practice hinders heaven.
These ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Application and initiative nourish wealth. Adornment and decoration nourish beauty. Suitable activity nourishes health. Good friendship nourishes ethical conduct. Sense restraint nourishes the spiritual life. Honesty nourishes friends. Rehearsing nourishes learning. Eagerness to listen and ask questions nourishes wisdom. Commitment and reviewing nourish good qualities. Right practice nourishes heaven.
These ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.”

1. Dasahi bhikkhave vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhamāno ariyasāvako ariyāya vaḍḍhiyā vaḍḍhati, sārādāyī ca hoti varā

These, <term>bhikkhus</term> <gloss>monks</gloss>, are the ten things that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world.

3. Regarding these ten things, <term>bhikkhus</term>, that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten things that act as obstacles:

4. Laziness and lack of effort are obstacles to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are obstacles to physical appearance. Unwholesome behavior is an obstacle to health. Bad friendship is an obstacle to moral conduct. Lack of restraint over the senses is an obstacle to the <term>brahmacariya</term> <gloss>the holy life or celibate life</gloss>. Deceitfulness is an obstacle to friendships. Lack of recitation is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are obstacles to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are obstacles to the <term>dhammas</term> <gloss>teachings or mental qualities</gloss>. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavenly realms.

Regarding these ten things, <term>bhikkhus</term>, that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world, these are the ten things that act as obstacles.

5. Regarding these ten things, <term>bhikkhus</term>, that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world, there are ten things that act as nutrients <note>original: āhārā; these are factors that sustain or nourish the growth of the desired qualities</note>:

6. Diligence and effort are the nutrients for wealth. Grooming and adornment are the nutrients for physical appearance. Wholesome behavior is the nutrient for health. Good friendship is the nutrient for moral conduct. Restraint over the senses is the nutrient for the holy life. Honesty is the nutrient for friendships. Recitation is the nutrient for great learning. The desire to listen and questioning are the nutrients for wisdom. Application and reflection are the nutrients for the teachings. Right practice is the nutrient for the heavenly realms.

Regarding these ten things, <term>bhikkhus</term>, that are desired, loved, and pleasant, but difficult to obtain in the world, these are the ten things that act as nutrients.

<summary>This page from the Anguttara Nikaya outlines ten desirable worldly qualities and identifies the specific obstacles that prevent them and the nourishing behaviors that foster them. It emphasizes practical habits like diligence, social connections, and mental reflection as the foundations for success in both worldly and spiritual life.</summary>
<keywords>Anguttara Nikaya, Buddhism, Pali Canon, wealth, health, moral conduct, wisdom, obstacles, nutrients, spiritual practice</keywords>

3. For these ten things, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and difficult to obtain in the world, ten things are obstacles <term>paripanthā</term> <gloss>obstructions or highway robbers</gloss>:

4. Laziness and lack of initiative are obstacles to wealth.
Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are obstacles to beauty.
Acting in ways that are not conducive to health <note>original: "asappāyakiriyā"</note> is an obstacle to health.
Bad friendship is an obstacle to virtue.
Lack of restraint of the senses is an obstacle to the holy life <term>brahmacariyassa</term> <gloss>the pure or celibate life</gloss>.
Deceitfulness is an obstacle to friendship.
Lack of recitation <note>repetitive oral practice</note> is an obstacle to great learning.
Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are obstacles to wisdom.
Lack of devotion and lack of reflection are obstacles to the teachings <term>dhammānam</term>.
Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten things that are obstacles to those ten things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and difficult to obtain in the world.

5. For these ten things, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and difficult to obtain in the world, ten things are nourishments <term>āhārā</term> <gloss>nutrients or supports</gloss>:

6. Lack of laziness and initiative are the nourishment for wealth.
Grooming and adornment are the nourishment for beauty.
Acting in ways conducive to health are the nourishment for health.
Good friendship is the nourishment for virtue.
Restraint of the senses is the nourishment for the holy life.
Honesty <note>literally: non-deceitfulness</note> is the nourishment for friendship.
Recitation is the nourishment for great learning.
Desire to listen and questioning are the nourishment for wisdom.
Devotion and reflection are the nourishment for the teachings.
Right practice is the nourishment for the heavenly realms.

These, monks, are the ten things that are the nourishments for those ten things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and difficult to obtain in the world.

<summary>This page from the Anguttara Nikaya lists the ten obstacles that prevent one from attaining worldly and spiritual goals, and the ten corresponding positive actions that support their attainment.</summary>
<keywords>Anguttara Nikaya, Buddhist ethics, obstacles, nourishment, wealth, wisdom, virtue, holy life, Pali Canon</keywords>

These ten qualities, monks, are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.

3. Regarding these ten qualities, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world, ten qualities are obstacles:

4. Laziness and lack of exertion are an obstacle to wealth. Lack of grooming and lack of adornment are an obstacle to beauty. Unwholesome action is an obstacle to health. Evil friendship is an obstacle to moral virtues. Lack of sense restraint is an obstacle to the holy life. Deception is an obstacle to friendships. Lack of recitation is an obstacle to great learning. Lack of desire to listen and lack of questioning are an obstacle to wisdom. Lack of application and lack of reflection are an obstacle to the teachings. Wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavens.

Regarding these ten qualities, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world, these ten qualities are obstacles.

5. Regarding these ten qualities, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world, ten qualities are supports:

6. Lack of laziness and exertion are a support for wealth. Grooming and adornment are a support for beauty. Wholesome action is a support for health. Good friendship is a support for moral virtues. Sense restraint is a support for the holy life. Honesty is a support for friendships. Recitation is a support for great learning. Desire to listen and questioning are a support for wisdom. Application and reflection are a support for the teachings. Right practice is a support for the heavens.

Regarding these ten qualities, monks, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world, these ten qualities are supports.

<margin>1. M. Ph. omit this phrase.</margin>
<margin>2. M. Ph. obstacles, and so throughout.</margin>
<margin>3. M. Ph. laziness throughout.</margin>
<margin>4. S. omits all from Lack of grooming to Lack of recitation.</margin>
<margin>5. T. beauty.</margin>
<margin>6. M. lack of sense restraint; T. M6 sense restraint.</margin>
<margin>7. T. lack of desire to listen.</margin>
<margin>8. M6. M, reflection; T. not reflecting.</margin>
<margin>9. T. M, lack of laziness.</margin>
<margin>10. all MSS. except S. put exertion before lack of laziness.</margin>
<margin>11. T. M6. M, reflection.</margin>

<summary>This page from the Anguttara Nikaya outlines ten desirable worldly qualities and identifies the specific behaviors that either obstruct or support their attainment. It emphasizes practical virtues such as exertion, sense restraint, and right practice as the foundations for success and spiritual progress.</summary>
<keywords>Anguttara Nikaya, ten qualities, obstacles, supports, wealth, health, wisdom, moral virtue, sense restraint, right practice</keywords>

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, adinnâdâyino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abrahmacârino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, musâvâdino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pisuṇâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pharusâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, samphappalâpino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abhijhâluno bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, vyâpannacittâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, micchâdiṭṭhikâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu. Pubbe katam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam² na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato aupapabhbiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu paṭhamo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

3. Tatra bhikkhave ye te samaṇabrâhmaṇâ evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti tyâham upasaṅkamitvâ evam vadâmi :—Saccam kira tumhe âyasmanto evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti?

Te ce me evam puṭṭhâ âmâ³ ti paṭijânanti.

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu . . . pe . . . micchâdiṭṭhino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu. Issaranimmânânam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato anupalabbhiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu dutiyo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

---

¹ All MSS. pisuṇâvâcâ and pharusâvâcâ (Comp. below XVI. 8).
² The MSS. here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.
³ D., T. âmo.

[context] There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:
[context] ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—has no cause or reason.’
[context] Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything an individual person experiences is because of past deeds, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of past deeds.’
Those who believe that past deeds are the most important thing have no enthusiasm or effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my first legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences is because of God Almighty’s creation, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of God Almighty’s creation.’
Those who believe that God Almighty’s creative power is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my second legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences has no cause or reason, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all without cause or reason.’
Those who believe that the absence of cause or reason is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
[context] This is my third legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
[context] These are the three sectarian tenets—as pursued, pressed, and grilled by the astute—which, when taken to their conclusion, end with inaction.
[context] But the Dhamma that I’ve taught is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.

# The Great Section <note>original: Mahā-vagga</note>

I say this to them: If that is so, venerable sirs, then people will be killers of living beings <term>pāṇātipātino</term> <gloss>those who take life</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be takers of what is not given <term>adinnādāyino</term> <gloss>thieves</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be unchaste <term>abrahmacārino</term> <gloss>those living a non-celibate life</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be speakers of lies <term>musāvādino</term> because of what was done in the past. They will use slanderous speech <term>pisuṇāvācā</term> <margin>All manuscripts read pisuṇāvācā and pharusāvācā. Compare below section XVI. 8.</margin> because of what was done in the past. They will use harsh speech <term>pharusāvācā</term> because of what was done in the past. They will engage in idle chatter <term>samphappalāpino</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be covetous <term>abhijjhāluno</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be ill-willed in mind <term>vyāpannacittā</term> because of what was done in the past. They will hold wrong views <term>micchādiṭṭhikā</term> because of what was done in the past.

But monks, for those who fall back on <margin>The manuscripts here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.</margin> what was done in the past as the essential truth <note>meaning they believe everything is predestined by past karma</note>, there is no desire to act, no effort, no sense that this should be done or this should not be done. Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics.

This, monks, is my first righteous refutation <term>sahadhammiko niggaho</term> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such theories.

3. Regarding this, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak and hold this view: Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <term>issaranimmānahetu</term> <gloss>the act of a creator god</gloss>. I go to them and say: Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a view?

When I ask them this, they acknowledge <margin>D. and T. manuscripts read āmo.</margin> it, saying: Yes.

I say to them: If that is so, venerable sirs, then people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... <note>the text repeats the previous list of ten unwholesome actions</note> ...they will hold wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. But monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is no desire to act, no effort, no sense that this should be done or this should not be done. Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics.

This, monks, is my second righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such theories.

<summary>The Buddha refutes the theories of fatalism based on past karma and creationism by a Supreme Lord. He argues these views lead to moral inaction and the abandonment of personal effort.</summary>
<keywords>karma, fatalism, creationism, morality, free will, unwholesome actions, Buddha, refutation</keywords>

### The Great Chapter <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

I say this to them: "Therefore, venerable sirs, you would become takers of life <term>pânâtipâtino</term> <gloss>those who kill living beings</gloss> because of what was done in the past. You would become takers of what is not given <term>adinnâdâyino</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become unchaste <term>abrahmacârino</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become speakers of lies <term>musâvâdino</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become speakers of slander <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> <margin>All manuscripts read pisuṇâvâcâ and pharusâvâcâ. Compare with section XVI. 8 below.</margin> because of what was done in the past. You would become speakers of harsh words <term>pharusâvâcâ</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become idle chatterers <term>samphappalâpino</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become covetous <term>abhijhâluno</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become ill-willed <term>vyâpannacittâ</term> because of what was done in the past. You would become holders of wrong views <term>micchâdiṭṭhikâ</term> because of what was done in the past." For those, monks, who rely on what was done in the past <margin>The manuscripts here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.</margin> as the essential truth, there is no desire, no effort, and no sense that "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Thus, when what should and should not be done is not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection cannot possess a legitimate, righteous claim to being a true ascetic.

This, monks, is my first righteous refutation <term>sahadhammiko niggaho</term> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

3. In that regard, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: "Whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <term>issaranimmânahetu</term>." I approach them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold the doctrine and view that whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

When they are asked this by me, they admit it, saying: "Yes" <margin>Manuscripts D. and T. read âmo.</margin>.

I say this to them: "Therefore, venerable sirs, you would become takers of life because of the creation of a Supreme Lord ... <note>The text repeats the previous list of ten unwholesome actions.</note> ... you would become holders of wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. For those, monks, who rely on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is no desire, no effort, and no sense that 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done.' Thus, when what should and should not be done is not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection cannot possess a legitimate, righteous claim to being a true ascetic."

This, monks, is my second righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such doctrines and views.

<summary>The Buddha refutes two fatalistic views: that all current experiences are determined by past actions or by a Supreme Lord's creation. He argues these views eliminate personal responsibility and the necessity for moral effort.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, karma, Supreme Lord, moral responsibility, ten unwholesome actions, refutation, asceticism</keywords>

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of what was done in the past, they will be takers of what is not given because of what was done in the past, they will be unchaste because of what was done in the past, they will be speakers of lies because of what was done in the past, <margin>All manuscripts read <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> and <term>pharusâvâcâ</term></margin> they will be speakers of malicious words because of what was done in the past, they will be speakers of harsh words because of what was done in the past, they will be idle chatterers because of what was done in the past, they will be covetous because of what was done in the past, they will be ill-willed because of what was done in the past, and they will be of wrong view because of what was done in the past. <margin>The manuscripts here and below vary between <term>gacchantam</term> and <term>gacchatam</term>.</margin> Monks, for those who fall back on what was done in the past as the essential truth, there is no desire, no effort, no 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done.' Thus, when what should and should not be done is not found to be true or certain, for those who live with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there is no legitimate, righteous claim to being a recluse."

Monks, this is my first righteous rebuttal to those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.

3. Regarding this, monks, there are those recluses and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view: "Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all of it is caused by the creation of a supreme deity." I go to them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold this doctrine and this view: 'Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all of it is caused by the creation of a supreme deity'?"

When I ask them this, if they acknowledge it, saying, "Yes." <margin>D. and T. manuscripts read <term>âmo</term>.</margin>

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a supreme deity... and so on... they will be of wrong view because of the creation of a supreme deity. Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a supreme deity as the essential truth, there is no desire, no effort, no 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done.' Thus, when what should and should not be done is not found to be true or certain, for those who live with muddled mindfulness and without protection, there is no legitimate, righteous claim to being a recluse."

Monks, this is my second righteous rebuttal to those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.

<summary>The Buddha critiques the views that human experience and moral actions are determined solely by past karma or by the will of a supreme deity. He argues that such fatalistic views negate the necessity of human effort and moral responsibility.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, karma, supreme deity, moral responsibility, Buddha, righteous rebuttal, asceticism</keywords>

Therefore he does not censure men, and men do not censure him. The perfect man does not seek to be heard of; how is it that you delight in doing so?'

Confucius said, 'Excellent;' and thereupon he took leave of his associates, forsook his disciples, retired to the neighbourhood of a great marsh, wore skins and hair cloth, and ate acorns and chestnuts. He went among animals without causing any confusion among their herds, and among birds without troubling their movements. Birds and beasts did not dislike him; how much less would men do so!

5. Confucius asked Ȝze-sang Hû, saying, 'I was twice driven from Lû; the tree was felled over me in Sung; I was obliged to disappear from Wei; I was reduced to extreme distress in Shang and Kâu; and I was kept in a state of siege between Khăn and Ȝhâi. I have encountered these various calamities; my intimate associates are removed from me more and more; my followers and friends are more and more dispersed;—why have all these things befallen me?'

<margin>呂註</margin>為學未聞道者也未聞道而求之不得不博故曰益為道者已聞道者也已聞道而為之不得不無為而已故曰損而又損者未免乎有為也并其損之者而損焉而後至於無為無為者寂然而不動之謂也無不為者感而遂通天下之故之謂也無為而至無為此之謂經學無憂謂之神神之為方也道之謂也至神其孰能與於此也由此觀之取天下常以無為及其有為不足以取天下可知已

<column-break/>

<margin>黃茂材註</margin>無所不知而後可以言學故學欲日益無所不為而後可以言道故道欲日損然益者可以進求而損者或難於強致唯至明者方能瞥地脫落乃至無為之地故能無所不為而應用不窮施於天下綽綽然矣

<margin>息齋註</margin>為學所以求知故日益為道所以去妄故日損知不極則損不全故日益者為日損之地也若損之又損妄去真全則無為矣至於無為則凡有為未嘗不無此又未易以損益論也及其無為之至雖天下之多而一貫之也若以有事而生事難暇前之一物尚膠纒乖錯而況天下之多乎

<meta>This page contains commentary on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The layout consists of four distinct commentaries by Su, Lü, Huang Maocai, and Xizhai followed by the main scripture text.</meta>

<margin>Commentary by Su <note>Su Che, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> One who does not know the Way but applies themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily, yet they have no means to unify it. This inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: To hear much and select what is good to follow, or to see much and remember it, is only the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back at falsehoods. Every false action is a delusion. To discard delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decrease." Confucius said to Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I permeate everything with a single thread. Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is what we call decrease. Once delusions no longer exist, and one has even forgotten the act of forgetting, the mind returns to nature entirely. Then one can act without departing from <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Because they create activities and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them. Therefore, success is difficult to achieve. The Sage practices non-action and thus has no ulterior motives in his heart. When his heart is visible externally, all things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Commentary by Lü <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a high official and scholar of the Song dynasty</note></margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they have not heard it, they must seek it broadly; thus it is said that learning "increases." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard the Way. Having heard it, they must practice it through non-action; thus it is said that the Way "decreases." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet escaped the realm of "doing." Only when one even decreases the act of decreasing does one reach the state of non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Doing nothing is left undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the causes under heaven. Moving from "doing" to "non-doing" is what is called the constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who can attain this level of divinity? From this we see that to take the world, one must always use non-action. If one uses "doing," it is clear they are not fit to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after being able to do anything can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly shed their attachments and reach the land of non-action. Thus they can do anything, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading across the world with ample room.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai <note>Likely the Daoist scholar Li Daichun, Yuan dynasty</note></margin> Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the Way is the means to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then decrease cannot be complete; thus daily increase provides the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then there is non-action. Upon reaching non-action, then all that is "done" has never not been "non-doing." This state cannot be easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, though the things of the world are many, a single thread permeates them. If one uses "business" to create more "business," it is difficult to find leisure. Even a single object can become entangled and chaotic, how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a cautious and clouded mind, making the heart of the world simple and whole. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>The text breaks here and continues on the next page.</note>
