<meta>This page contains commentary on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The layout consists of four distinct commentaries by Su, Lü, Huang Maocai, and Xizhai, followed by the main text of Chapter 49.</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> One who does not know the Way <term>Dao</term> but devotes themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. However, without a single principle to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: Hear much and select what is good to follow; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back at falsehoods. Every false action is a delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? He replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I pervade everything with a single principle. To forget the mind in order to restore nature purely is what is meant by "decreasing." If delusions still remain, one must continue until both are forgotten. When the mind is purified and nature is restored without remnant, one abandons forced action <term>wei</term> and attains non-action <term>wu wei</term>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Therefore, when they create trouble and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them; thus they find it difficult to achieve their goals. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no concerns in his heart. His inner state is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a key figure in the New Policies of the Song dynasty.</note></margin> Those who practice learning are those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they have not heard the Way, they must seek it broadly; therefore, it is said that they "increase." Those who practice the Way are those who have already heard it. Having heard it, they must practice it by doing nothing other than non-action; therefore, it is said that they "decrease." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet avoided having some action. One must even decrease the act of decreasing itself. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action refers to being silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" refers to being moved and then penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is what is called the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we can see that taking the world is always done through non-action. When one relies on forced action, it is clear they are insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar known for his works on the Laozi.</note></margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires daily increase. Only after reaching a state where nothing is forced can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those of supreme clarity can suddenly cast off burdens and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they act with ample freedom.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>The art name of Wang Tingzhen, a Yuan dynasty scholar.</note></margin> One practices learning to seek knowledge, thus it increases daily. One practices the Way to remove delusion, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never not been non-action. This state cannot be easily discussed in terms of decrease or increase. When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast, it is unified by a single principle. If one creates trouble through busy-ness, then even a single object in front of them remains entangled and chaotic, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart; he takes the heart of the people as his own heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue is goodness. To those who are trustworthy, I trust them. To those who are not trustworthy, I also trust them; thus virtue is trust. The Sage is in the world, blending his heart with the world to make it whole. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him. The Sage <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<margin>Su's Commentary</margin> Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> and devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily, yet they have nothing to unify it; this inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much and select what is good to follow; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the <term>Tao</term>, you look back at all that was false; everything done was nothing but delusion. To remove delusion and return to nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it with one principle." Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is what is called decreasing; yet as long as delusions remain, one must reach the point of forgetting the mind itself to purely return to nature. Only when nothing remains do you leave behind "doing" and yet do not fail at "non-doing." Everyone has the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus they create tasks and seek results. When this intention is seen outwardly, things resist it; therefore it is difficult and cannot be achieved. The Sage practices non-doing, so his mind is without affairs. When this is seen outwardly, things are at peace with him. Although he does not "take" the world's affairs to act upon them, the affairs of the world find order and peace therein.

<margin>Lü's Commentary</margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have not heard the <term>Tao</term> and seek it cannot avoid being broad, hence it is called "daily increase." Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have heard the <term>Tao</term> and practice it cannot avoid simply practicing non-doing, hence it is called "daily decrease." To decrease and further decrease is for those who have not yet escaped "doing." When even the one who decreases is himself decreased, only then does one arrive at non-doing. Non-doing means being still and unmoving. Doing nothing left undone means being stimulated and thereby penetrating all the causes under heaven. Arriving at non-doing through non-doing is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called the Divine. The direction of the Divine is what is called the <term>Tao</term>. As for the Supreme Divine, who can partake in this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-doing. By the time one resorts to "doing," it is clear they are insufficient to take the world.

Only the most enlightened can suddenly shed everything and reach the realm of non-doing. 寶釵聽了，忙命鶯兒去找了兩丸來與平兒。寶釵道：「既這樣，你去替我問候罷，我就不去了。」平兒向寶釵答應著去了。不在話下。

且說香菱見了眾人之後，吃過晚飯，寶釵等都往買母處去，自己便往瀟湘館中來。此時黛玉已好了大半了，見香菱也進園來住，自是喜歡。香菱因笑道：「我這一進來了，也得空兒，好歹教我做詩，就是我的造化了！」黛玉笑道：「既要學做詩，你就拜我為師。我雖不通，大略也還教的起你。」香菱笑道：「果然這樣，我就拜你為師，你可不許厭煩的。」黛玉道：「什麼難事，也值得去學？不過是起承轉合。當中承轉，是兩副對子：平聲的對仄聲；虛的對實的，實的對虛的。若是果有了奇句，連平仄虛實不對都使的的。」

香菱笑道：「怪道我常弄本舊詩偷兒看一兩首，又有對的極工的，又有不對的；又聽見說，『一三五不論，二四六分明，』看古人的詩上，亦有順的，亦有二四六上錯的：所以天天疑惑。如今聽你一說，原來這些規矩竟是沒事的，只要詞句新奇為上。」黛玉道：「正是這個道理。詞句究竟還是末事，第一是立意要緊。若意趣真了，連詞句不用修飾，自是好的：這叫做『不為辭害意』。」

香菱道：「我只愛陸放翁的『重簾不卷留香久，古硯微凹聚墨多』，說的真切有趣！」黛玉道：「你們因不知詩，所以見了這淺近的就愛。一入了這個格局，再學不出來的。你只聽我說：你若真心要學，我這裡有《王摩詰全集》，你且把他的五言律一百首細心揣摩透熟了，然後再讀一百二十首老杜的七言律，次之再李青蓮的七言絕句讀一二百首。肚子裡先有了這三個人做了底子，然後再陶淵明、應、劉、謝、阮、庾、鮑等人的一看。你又是這樣一個極聰明伶俐的人，不用一年工夫，不愁不是詩翁了！」香菱聽了，笑道：「既這樣，好姑娘，你就這書給我出來，我帶回去，夜裡念幾首也是好的。」黛玉聽說，便命紫鵑將王右丞的五言律拿來，遞與香菱，道：「你只看有紅圈的，都是我選的，有一首念一首。不明白的，問你姑娘；或者遇見我，我講與你就是了。」

香菱拿了詩，回至蘅蕪院中，諸事不管，只向燈下一首一首的讀起來。寶釵連催他數次睡覺，他也不睡。寶釵見他這般苦心，只得隨他去了。

一日，黛玉方梳洗完了，只見香菱吟吟的送了書來，又要換杜律。黛玉笑道：「共記得多少首？」香菱笑道：「凡紅圈選的，我盡讀了。」黛玉道：「可領略了些沒有？」香菱笑道：「我倒領略了些，只不知不是，說給你聽聽。」

He didn't, however, drag him down and strike him with a rattan or cane, but recklessly assaulted him, while he stood before him, with something or other, which he laid hold of, and broke his face open in two places. We understand that Mrs. Hsüeh has in here some medicine or other for applying on wounds, so do try, miss, and find a ball of it and let me have it!"

Hearing this, Pao-ch'ai speedily directed Ying Erh to go and look for some, and, on discovering two balls of it, she brought them over and handed them to P'ing Erh.

"Such being the case," Pao-ch'ai said, "do make, on your return, the usual inquiries for me, and I won't then need to go."

P'ing Erh turned towards Pao-ch'ai, and expressed her readiness to execute her commission, after which she betook herself home, where we will leave her without further notice.

After Hsiang Ling, for we will take up the thread of our narrative with her, completed her visits to the various inmates, she had her evening meal. Then when Pao-ch'ai and every one else went to dowager lady Chia's quarters, she came into the Hsiao Hsiang lodge. By this time Tai-yü had got considerably better. Upon hearing that Hsiang Ling had also moved into the garden, she, needless to say, was filled with delight.

"Now, that I've come in here," Hsiang Ling then smiled and said, "do please teach me, at your leisure, how to write verses. It will be a bit of good luck for me if you do."

"Since you're anxious to learn how to versify," Tai-yü answered with a smile, "you'd better acknowledge me as your tutor; for though I'm not a good hand at poetry, yet I know, after all, enough to be able to teach you."

"Of course you do!" Hsiang Ling laughingly remarked. "I'll readily treat you as my tutor. But you mustn't put yourself to any trouble!"

"Is there anything so difficult about this," Tai-yü pursued, "as to make it necessary to go in for any study? Why, it's purely and simply a matter of openings, elucidations, embellishments and conclusions. The elucidations and embellishments, which come in the centre, should form two antithetical sentences, the even tones must pair with the uneven. Empty words must correspond with full words; and full words with empty words. In the event of any out-of-the-way lines, it won't matter if the even and uneven tones, and the empty and full words do not pair."

"Strange though it may appear," smiled Hsiang Ling, "I often handle books with old poems, and read one or two stanzas, whenever I can steal the time; and some among these I find pair most skilfully, while others don't. I have also heard that the first, third and fifth lines are of no consequence; and that the second, fourth and sixth must be clearly distinguished. But I notice that there are in the poetical works of ancient writers both those which accord with the rules, as well as those whose second, fourth and sixth lines are not in compliance with any rule. Hence it is that my mind has daily been full of doubts. But after the hints you've given me, I really see that all these formulas are of no account, and that the main requirement is originality of diction."

"Yes, that's just the principle that holds good," Tai-yü answered. "But diction is, after all, a last consideration. The first and foremost thing is the choice of proper sentiments; for when the sentiments are correct, there'll even be no need to polish the diction; it's certain to be elegant. This is called versifying without letting the diction affect the sentiments."

"What I admire," Hsiang Ling proceeded with a smile; "are the lines by old Lu Fang;

"The double portière, when not raised, retains the fragrance long.
An old inkslab, with a slight hole, collects plenty of ink.

"Their language is so clear that it's charming."

"You must on no account," Tai-yü observed, "read poetry of the kind. It's because you people don't know what verses mean that you, no sooner read any shallow lines like these, than they take your fancy. But when once you get into this sort of style, it's impossible to get out of it. Mark my words! If you are in earnest about learning, I've got here Wang Mo-chieh's complete collection; so you'd better take his one hundred stanzas, written in the pentameter rule of versification, and carefully study them, until you apprehend them thoroughly. Afterwards, look over the one hundred and twenty stanzas of Lao T'u, in the heptameter rule; and next read a hundred or two hundred of the heptameter four-lined stanzas by Li Ch'ing-lieu. When you have, as a first step, digested these three authors, and made them your foundation, you can take T'ao Yuan-ming, Ying, Liu, Hsieh, Yüan, Yü, Pao and other writers and go through them once. And with those sharp and quick wits of yours, I've no doubt but that you will become a regular poet before a year's time."

"Well, in that case," Hsiang Ling smiled, after listening to her, "bring me the book, my dear miss, so that I may take it along. It will be a good thing if I can manage to read several stanzas at night."

At these words, Tai-yü bade Tzu Chüan fetch Wang Tso-ch'eng's pentameter stanzas. When brought, she handed them to Hsiang Ling. "Only peruse those marked with red circles" she said. "They've all been selected by me. Read each one of them; and should there be any you can't fathom, ask your miss about them. Or when you come across me, I can explain them to you."

Hsiang Ling took the poems and repaired back to the Heng Wu-yüan. And without worrying her mind about anything she approached the lamp and began to con stanza after stanza. Pao-ch'ai pressed her, several consecutive times, to go to bed; but as even rest was far from her thoughts, Pao-ch'ai let her, when she perceived what trouble she was taking over her task, have her own way in the matter.

Tai-yü had one day just finished combing her hair and performing her ablutions, when she espied Hsiang Ling come with smiles playing about her lips, to return her the book and to ask her to let her have T'u's poetical compositions in exchange.

"Of all these, how many stanzas can you recollect?" Tai-yü asked, smiling.

"I've read every one of those marked with a red circle," Hsiang Ling laughingly rejoined.

"Have you caught the ideas of any of them, yes or no?" Tai-yü inquired.

"Yes, I've caught some!" Hsiang Ling smiled. "But whether rightly or not I don't know. Let me tell you."

<meta>continues from previous page: the account of the domestic conflict involving Ping’er and the violence she endured.</meta>

<note>The speaker is describing a beating Ping’er received.</note>
"They turned the boards and sticks upside down and beat her while she stood there. I do not know what implement they used, but they struck her a great deal and cut her face in two places. We heard that you, Ma'am <note>referring to Aunt Xue, Xue Baochai’s mother</note>, have a certain medicine here for treating staff wounds. Would you find a pill for me, Miss?"

Upon hearing this, Baochai quickly ordered Ying'er to find two pills and give them to Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, go and give her my regards for me; I shall not go myself." Ping'er assented to Baochai and departed. This matter requires no further detail.

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, and while Baochai and the others went to Lady Wang's quarters, she made her way to the Bamboo Lodge <note>original: "Xiaoxiang Guan", the residence of Lin Daiyu</note>. By this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had come to live in the garden, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I have moved in and have some free time, if you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" 

Daiyu laughed and replied, "Since you wish to learn poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not truly proficient, I know enough to teach you the basics." 

Xiangling smiled and said, "If that is truly so, I shall take you as my master. You must not grow weary of me."

Daiyu said, "What difficulty is there in it that it should be so hard to learn? It is nothing more than the <term>Qi-Cheng-Zhuan-He</term> <gloss>Introduction, Elucidation, Transition, and Conclusion</gloss>. The middle sections, the elucidation and transition, consist of two sets of couplets: level tones against deflected tones, empty words against solid words, and solid against empty. If you truly have a remarkable line, you can even ignore the rules of tonal balance and formal structure."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder I often peek at one or two poems in old books and find some that are perfectly balanced while others are not. I have also heard it said that 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow this and others are wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. I have been puzzled every day. Now that I hear you speak, it seems these rules do not matter much after all, as long as the phrasing is novel and original."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the point. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; the most important thing is the intent. If the intent and the mood are genuine, the poem will be good even without polished phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning.'"

Xiangling said, "I simply love Lu Fangweng's <note>the poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the old inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu replied, "Because you do not yet understand poetry, you like what is shallow and accessible. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to escape it. Listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the <term>Wang Mojie Quanji</term> <gloss>The Collected Works of Wang Wei</gloss>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and study them until you have thoroughly mastered them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>referring to Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>referring to Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. With the work of these three as your foundation, you can then look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Since you are such an exceptionally clever and bright person, in less than a year’s time, you need not worry about not becoming a true poet!" 

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled and said, "In that case, dear Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems at night." 

Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Wei's five-character regulated poems and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at those marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Alpinia Park <note>original: "Hengwu Yuan", Baochai’s residence</note>. Ignoring all other affairs, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such devotion, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, Xiangling arrived with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. 

Daiyu asked with a smile, "How many do you remember?" 

Xiangling smiled and said, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." 

Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insight from them?" 

Xiangling laughed, "I have indeed gained some insight, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you what I think."

Xiangling laughed and replied, "If that is really the case, I shall take you as my teacher. You must not find me tiresome."

Xiangling smiled and said, "No wonder! I often used to steal a look at one or two poems in an old book. Some couplets were perfectly crafted, while others did not match at all. I also heard it said that 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Now that I hear you say it, it turns out these rules are actually flexible, and that fresh and original phrasing is what matters most."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; the most important thing is the conception. If the intent and interest are genuine, the poem will be good even without polishing the words. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning.'"

Xiangling said, "I simply love Lu Fangweng's <note>the poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu replied, "It is because you do not yet understand poetry that you love such shallow and simple things. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to learn your way out of it. Listen to me: if you are sincere about learning, I have here the *Complete Works of Wang Mojie* <note>the poet Wang Wei</note>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and contemplate them until you know them thoroughly. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems. After that, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have the foundation of these three men in your belly, you can look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. As you are such an extremely clever and sharp person, in less than a year’s time, you need not worry about becoming a true poet!"

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled and said, "In that case, dear Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems tonight." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of Wang Youcheng <note>Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you see me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Garden of Plantain Savory. Neglecting all other matters, she sat under the lamp and began to read them poem by poem. Baochai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such dedication, Baochai had no choice but to leave her be.

One day, just after Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, Xiangling arrived with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu asked with a smile, "How many do you remember?"

Xiangling smiled and said, "I have read all of those marked with red circles."

Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insights?"

Xiangling smiled and said, "I have indeed gained some understanding, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you about it."

Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the <term>Complete Works of Wang Mojie</term>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and ponder them until you know them thoroughly. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's seven-character regulated poems, followed by one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three as a foundation in your belly, then look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and others. Being as clever and sharp as you are, in less than a year’s work, you need not worry about not becoming a master poet!" Hearing this, Xiangling smiled, "If so, dear Miss, please bring those books out for me. I will take them back and it will be good to recite a few poems at night." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of Wang the Right Vice-President and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at those with red circles; I selected those myself. Read them one by one. If there is something you do not understand, ask your mistress, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Alpinia Park. Ignoring all other matters, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such painstaking dedication, Baochai had to let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, Xiangling came in smiling to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu smiled and asked, "How many poems do you remember in total?" Xiangling smiled, "I have read all those marked with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insight?" Xiangling smiled, "I have gained some insight, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you about it."

[context] But he had particularly cultivated logic, and was profoundly skilled in the interpretation of the holy Scriptures;
insomuch that the heretic Eunomius often shrank from the acumen which his reasoning displayed. As regards his diet he was not simple; for although he practised the strictest moderation, yet his table was always sumptuously furnished. He was also accustomed to indulge himself by wearing white garments, and bathing twice a day in the public baths. And when some one asked him 'why he, a bishop, bathed himself twice a day?' he replied, 'Because it is inconvenient to bathe thrice.' Going one day from courtesy to visit the bishop Arsacius, he was asked by one of the friends of that bishop, 'why he wore a garment so unsuitable for a bishop? And where it was written that an ecclesiastic should be clothed in white?' 'Do you tell me first,' said he, 'where it is written that a bishop should wear black?' When he that made the inquiry knew not what to reply to this counter-question: 'You cannot show,' rejoined Sisinnius, 'that a priest should be clothed in black. But Solomon is my authority, whose exhortation is, Let your garments be white.
And our Saviour in the Gospels appears clothed in white raiment: moreover he showed Moses and Elias to the apostles, clad in white garments.' His prompt reply to these and other questions called forth the admiration of those present. Again when Leontius bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, who had taken away a church from the Novatians, was on a visit to Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him, and begged him to restore the church. But he received him rudely, saying, 'You Novatians ought not to have churches; for you take away repentance, and shut out Divine mercy.' As Leontius gave utterance to these and many other such revilings against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied: 'No one repents more heartily than I do.' And when Leontius asked him 'Why do you repent?' 'That I came to see you,' said he. On one occasion John the bishop having a contest with him, said, 'The city cannot have two bishops.' 'Nor has it,' said Sisinnius. John being irritated at this response, said, 'You see you pretend that you alone are the bishop.' 'I do not say that,' rejoined Sisinnius; 'but that I am not bishop in your estimation only, who am such to others.' John being still more chafed at this reply, said, 'I will stop your preaching; for you are a heretic.' To which Sisinnius good-humoredly replied, 'I will give you a reward, if you will relieve me from so arduous a duty.' John being softened a little by this answer, said, 'I will not make you cease to preach, if you find speaking so troublesome.' So facetious was Sisinnius, and so ready at repartee: but it would be tedious to dwell further on his witticisms. Wherefore by means of a few specimens we have illustrated what sort of a person he was, deeming these as sufficient. I will merely add that he was celebrated for erudition, and on account of it all the bishops who succeeded him loved and honored him; and not only they but all the leading members of the senate also esteemed and admired him. He is the author of many works: but they are characterized by too great an affectation of elegance of diction, and a lavish intermingling of poetic expressions. On which account he was more admired as a speaker than as a writer; for there was dignity in his countenance and voice, as well as in his form and aspect, and every movement of his person was graceful. On account of these features he was loved by all the sects, and he was in special favor with Atticus the bishop. But I must conclude this brief notice of Sisinnius.
Not long after the death of John, the Emperor Arcadius died also.

it often happened that he would flee from those who possessed great skill in dialectic. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple, yet within extreme temperance, he made use of expensive things. He took pleasure in white clothing and continued to bathe twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third time. At another time, while he was seeing Bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of Arsacius’s followers why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should clothe himself in white. He said: You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing. When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius <note>Sisinnius was the Novatian bishop in Constantinople known for his wit and learning</note> followed up on his counter-question: You would not be able to show that a priest must be clothed in black. But Solomon advised me, saying: Let your garments be white <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah wearing white to the apostles. Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>specifically Little Galatia</note>, took away a church from the Novatians while he was visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius came to him and requested him to return the church. But Leontius answered warmly and said to him: You Novatians <note>a rigorist Christian sect that refused readmission to those who lapsed during persecution</note> ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied: Indeed, no one has repented as much as I have. When the other asked again: How have you repented? Sisinnius answered: Because I saw you.

Once when John <note>John Chrysostom, the Bishop of Constantinople</note> was accusing him of something and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: Indeed it does not. John became angry and said: You see that you alone are a bishop by your own counsel. Sisinnius replied: I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop to you alone, as I am to the ears of others. John, being provoked by what was said, replied: I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic. To this, Sisinnius answered gracefully: I will even give you a reward if you release me from such great labor. John, softened by the response, said: I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking grieves you at all.

Thus Sisinnius was ready with responses and full of grace. To write and record all the things spoken by him would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown through these few examples what kind of man he was to have been chosen to lead. I say this: everyone knows him for his education, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the illustrious members of the Senate loved and admired him. Many books were written by him, using a style where he mixes in poetic expressions. He was admired more when speaking than when being read; for such grace was in him—in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religions <note>referring to various Christian sects and perhaps non-Christians</note>, and especially by Bishop Atticus. Such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

[context] For as diseases arising from depraved meat and drink, from Animals, Vegetables, and fruites of the Earth; with Arcanums of Herbs and Roots are healed; so if from Mettals and Minerals, with their Arcanums also, in such Arcanums of Vegetables are refused. In the same manner
plainly, the greatest part of diseases, coming from Celestial Influence, and from the Astral Impression of the greater and lesser Worlds firmament, admit not of cure with promiscuous Remedies, as by Arcanums of Herbs, Minerals, and Metalls, but by Astronomick Influence, the cure is instituted with such things only as have an Analogy to the greater and lesser World, in which is the true Magnetick force of the Firmament, and a Celestial Impression of resisting diseases, caused by the Firmament of the greater and lesser World, as is apparent in Arsemart, the greater Comphry, Dragonwort, and the greater Wallwort. If supernaturally, the disease or dolour take its beginning from Inchantment or by Magical Impression of Ascendants, the endeavouring the Cure by the three former ways is fruitless and unprofitable; but according to Paracelsus, process must be made Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil by the same means it was inferr'd must again be expell'd. In the aforesaid Simples there is an Influential Attractive, and all according to Divine Ordination, Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically cure; because in them is Medicine, and in Man the Magnet.
For as the Sun and Stars have power of attracting humidity from Inferiours, so Man (by the Magnetick attractive virtue placed in him, attracts Spirit instead of Nutriment, as a Loadstone draws Iron) and Inferiors have the same power of attracting from Superiors, as we see in time of the Pest; and these
[margin] ... Astral, Venenate, and Spiritual, the fift is such as are inflicted as a Scourge.

[context] And they named Barnabas the Lord of the Gods; and Paul Hermes,
because he commenced the speaking.
And the priest of the Lord of the Gods, who was without the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gate of the court where they lodged, and was disposed to offer sacrifices to them.
But Barnabas and Paul, when they heard [it], rent their garments, and sprang and went among the throng, and called out, and said: Men, what do ye? We also are frail mortals like yourselves, who preach to you, that ye should turn from these useless things, unto the living God, who made heaven and earth and seas, and whatever is in them.
He, in former ages, left all the nations to go in their own ways: although he did not leave himself without testimony, while he did them good from heaven, and sent down the rain, and made the fruits to grow in their seasons, and filled their hearts with food and pleasure.
And, by saying these things, they with difficulty prevented the people from offering sacrifice to them.
But Jews came hither from Iconium and Antioch, and excited the people against them. And they stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
And the disciples assembled around him; and he arose, and went into the city. And the next day, he departed from there, with Barnabas; and they came to the city of Derbe.
And while they were preaching to the inhabitants of that city, they made many disciples. And turning back, they came to the city Lystra, and to Iconium, and to Antioch,
[context] confirming the souls of the disciples, and entreating them to persevere in the faith; and they told them, that it was necessary, through much affliction, to enter into the kingdom of God.

There may be similarity in understanding without similarity in outward form. There may also be similarity in form without similarity in understanding. The Sage embraces similarity of understanding and pays no regard to similarity of form. The world in general is attracted by similarity of form, but remains indifferent to similarity of understanding. Those creatures that resemble them in shape they love and consort with; those that differ from them in shape they fear and keep at a distance. The creature that has a skeleton seven feet long, hands differently shaped from the feet, hair on its head, and an even set of teeth in its jaws, and walks erect, is called a man. But it does not follow that a man may not have the mind of a brute. Even though this be the case, other men will still recognise him as one of their own species in virtue of his outward form. Creatures which have wings on the back or horns on the head, serrated teeth or extensile talons, which fly overhead or run on all fours, are called birds and beasts. But it does not follow that a bird or a beast may not have the mind of a man. Yet, even if this be so, it is nevertheless assigned to another species because of the difference in form. P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes. Howbeit, in seeking perfect wisdom, men attend to the outward form alone, which will not bring them near to it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'uan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music. When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phoenix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music.

<meta>The text continues the philosophical discussion from the Book of Liezi, specifically within the Yellow Emperor chapter, regarding the distinction between external appearance and internal nature.</meta>

Even if they do not necessarily lack the heart of a beast, though they possess a beast's heart, they are treated with affection because of their outward form. It is said that those with horns, spreading teeth, extended claws, those that fly upward or crawl downward, are called birds and beasts; yet they do not necessarily lack the heart of a human. Though they may possess a human heart, they are treated with distance because of their outward form. <term>Paoxi</term> <gloss>Fuxi</gloss>, <term>Nuwa</term>, <term>Shennong</term>, and the Lord of <term>Xia</term> <gloss>Yu the Great</gloss> had bodies like snakes, faces like humans, heads like oxen, or noses like tigers. These possessed forms that were not human, yet they possessed the virtue of great sages. <term>Jie</term> of the Xia dynasty, <term>Zhou</term> of the Yin dynasty, <term>Huan</term> of Lu, and <term>Mu</term> of Chu had appearances and facial features <note>literally "seven orifices"</note> that were all identical to other humans, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the common people look only at a single outward form to seek the highest wisdom, they will likely never find it.

<margin>These two meanings are acceptable</margin>
<margin>Liezi: Yellow Emperor</margin>

The Yellow Emperor fought with the Flame Emperor <note>Yandi</note> in the wilds of <term>Banquan</term>. He led bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>a mythical auspicious beast</gloss>, and tigers as his front guard; eagles, black eagles, hawks, and kites served as his banners. This is an example of using power to command birds and beasts. <term>Yao</term> commanded <term>Kui</term> <note>a legendary music master</note> to manage the music. When stones were struck and tapped <note>referring to lithophones</note>, the hundred beasts led each other in dance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> music <note>the music of the sage king Shun</note> was performed nine times, the phoenixes came to present themselves.

<summary>This passage argues that internal virtue and external appearance are often mismatched, noting that ancient sages often had animal-like features while tyrants looked human. It also describes the ability of ancient sage-kings to command and harmonize with wild animals through power or music.</summary>
<keywords>Liezi, Fuxi, Shennong, Yellow Emperor, Banquan, virtue vs appearance, sage-kings, ancient mythology, music and animals</keywords>

<meta>This page is from the Yellow Emperor chapter of the Liezi, discussing the distinction between outward appearance and inner nature in humans and animals.</meta>

Even if they do not necessarily possess the hearts of beasts, those with the appearance of beasts will be treated as such because of how they look. There is a tradition that creatures with horns, separated teeth, spread claws, those that fly upward, or those that crawl and walk are called birds and beasts. Yet they do not necessarily lack the hearts of humans. 

Conversely, though some may have the hearts of humans, they are kept at a distance because of their appearance. The sovereign <term>Paoxi</term> <gloss>Fuxi</gloss>, the goddess <term>Nüwa</term>, the Divine Farmer <term>Shennong</term>, and the lords of the Xia dynasty had bodies like snakes, faces of humans, heads like oxen, or noses like tigers. These possessed appearances that were not human, yet they possessed the virtue of great sages. 

Xia Jie, Yin Zhou, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu <note>infamous tyrants and failed rulers of Chinese history</note> all had appearances and facial features <note>literally: the seven openings of the head</note> identical to other humans, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the masses rely solely on a single outward appearance to seek supreme wisdom, they will never come close to finding it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought against the Flame Emperor <note>Yandi</note> in the wilds of Banquan, he led bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>mythological fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, while using eagles, hawks, and kites as his banners. This was an instance of using power to command birds and beasts. When Yao appointed Kui to direct the music, and the sounding stones were struck and tapped, the hundred animals all danced together. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>music of Shun</gloss> was performed in nine movements, the phoenixes came to pay court.

<margin>Both of these meanings are acceptable.</margin>
<margin>Liezi: The Yellow Emperor.</margin>

<summary>This passage argues that internal virtue and intelligence are independent of physical appearance, citing sage-kings with animal traits and tyrants with human forms. It also describes how ancient rulers used music and power to influence the animal kingdom.</summary>
<keywords>Liezi, Yellow Emperor, Fuxi, Shennong, animal nature, sagehood, virtue versus appearance, Banquan, ancient music</keywords>

PEACEFUL LIFE.

Mazgusri, the prince royal, said to the Lord: It is difficult, Lord, most difficult, what these Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas will attempt out of reverence for the Lord. How are these Bodhisattvas MahAsattvas to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period? Whereupon the Lord answered Mazgusri, the prince royal: A Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Mazgusri, he who is to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period, must be firm in four things. In which things? The Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, must be firm in his conduct and proper sphere if he wishes to teach this Dharmaparyaya. And how, Maggusri, is a Bodhisattva Mahasattva firm in his conduct and proper sphere? When the Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Ma#gusri, is patient, meek, has reached the stage of meekness ; when he is not rash, nor envious; when, moreover, Mazigusri, he clings to no law whatever and sees the real character of the laws (or things) ; when he is refraining from investigating and discussing these laws, Mazigusri; that is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva. And what is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Mazgusri ? When the Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, does not serve, not court, not wait upon kings; does not serve, not court, not wait upon princes; when he does not approach them; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon persons of another sect, Aarakas, Parivragakas, Agivakas, Nirgranthas, nor persons passionately fond of fine literature; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon adepts at worldly spells, and votaries of a worldly philosophy, nor keep any intercourse with them ; when he does not go to see KAndalas, jugglers, vendors of pork, poulterers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors and dancers, wrestlers, nor resort to places whither others flock for amusement and sport; when he keeps no intercourse with them unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and that freely; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon monks, nuns, lay devotees, male and female, who are adherents of the vehicle of disciples, nor keep intercourse with them ; when he does not come in contact with them at the place of promenade or in the monastery, unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and even that freely. This, Mazgusri, is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdasattva.

Again, Maagusri, the Bodhisattva Mahdasattva does not take hold of some favourable opportunity or another to preach the law to females every now and anon, nor is he desirous of repeatedly seeing females ; nor does he think it proper to visit families and then too often address a girl, virgin, or young wife, nor does he greet them too fondly in return. He does not preach the law to a hermaphrodite, keeps no intercourse with such a person, nor greets too friendly in return. He does not enter a house alone in order to receive alms, unless having the Tathagata in his thoughts. And when he happens to preach the law to females, he does not do so by passionate attachment to the law, far less by passionate attachment to a woman. When he is preaching, he does not display his row of teeth, let alone a quick emotion on his physiognomy. He addresses no novice, male or female, no nun, no monk, no young boy, no young girl, nor enters upon a conversation with them; he shows no great readiness in answering their address, nor cares to give too frequent answers. This, Ma#gusri, is called the first proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

<margin>K 275</margin>

Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Youthful, spoke thus to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, it is difficult, truly very difficult, for these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to enlightenment</gloss> <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> to endure this out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, O Blessed One, should this <term>Dharma-paryaya</term> <gloss>Discourse of the Great Law</gloss> be proclaimed by these Bodhisattva Mahasattvas in the latter age, in the latter time?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Manjushri, the Ever-Youthful: "A Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in four qualities, Manjushri, should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. What are these four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association should proclaim this Discourse of the Great Law in the latter age, in the latter time. And how, Manjushri, does a Bodhisattva Mahasattva become established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association?

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, has reached the level of the disciplined, whose mind is neither terrified nor startled, and who is not envious; and when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not practice within the field of any particular phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note>, but views the true nature <note>original: "yatha-bhutam"</note> of all things according to their own characteristics. That which involves no fixation and no conceptualization regarding these things—this, Manjushri, is called the proper conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva?
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not serve a king, nor serve, associate with, attend upon, or approach princes, high ministers, or royal officials. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon followers of other schools, such as wandering mendicants <note>original: "caraka-parivrajaka"</note>, the <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a fatalist sect</gloss>, or the <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>the Jains</gloss>, nor those beings devoted to worldly poetry and treatises. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon those who hold to the spells of the materialists <note>original: "lokayata"</note>, nor those who follow materialism, nor does he become intimate with them.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, boxers, swine-breeders, poultry-keepers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or play belonging to others, nor does he become intimate with them. Only when such people have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment.

<margin>N 181</margin>
Furthermore, he does not serve, associate with, or attend upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who belong to the <term>Sravaka-yana</term> <gloss>the Disciple Vehicle/Hinayana</gloss>, nor does he become intimate with them. He does not share the same sphere of movement with them, whether in a walking path or in a monastery. Only when they have approached him does he preach the Law to them from time to time, and he preaches it without attachment. This, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not preach the Law frequently to women by seizing upon the signs of attraction for one reason or another, nor does he constantly desire the sight of women. He does not enter the homes of families, nor does he think he must frequently converse with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Law to eunuchs, nor does he become intimate with them or exchange greetings with them. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is practicing the <term>Tathagatanusmriti</term> <gloss>mindfulness of the Buddha</gloss>. Even if he preaches the Law to women, he does not preach it with any passion for the Law, much less...

<summary>The Buddha instructs Manjushri on the four qualities required to preach the Lotus Sutra in the future age of decline, specifically detailing the proper conduct and social boundaries a Bodhisattva must maintain. This includes avoiding worldly powers, rival sects, lower-caste occupations, and inappropriate intimacy with women or followers of the Hinayana.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Bodhisattva conduct, proper sphere of association, Sravaka-yana, latter age, monastic discipline</keywords>

->Chapter 13: The Chapter on Peaceful Practices<-

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Youthful, spoke to the Blessed One: Lord, it is difficult, extremely difficult, what these <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings seeking awakening</gloss> and <term>mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> have undertaken out of reverence for the Blessed One. Lord, how should this <term>dharmaparyaya</term> <gloss>exposition of the Law/Lotus Sutra</gloss> be proclaimed by these bodhisattvas and mahasattvas in the later times, in the final age? 

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to Manjushri, the Ever-Youthful: Manjushri, when established in four principles, a bodhisattva and mahasattva should proclaim this exposition of the Law in the later times, in the final age. Which four? Here, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva who is established in proper conduct <note>original: "acara"</note> and proper sphere of association <note>original: "gocara"</note> should proclaim this exposition of the Law in the later times, in the final age. 

And how, Manjushri, is a bodhisattva and mahasattva established in proper conduct and proper sphere of association? When a bodhisattva and mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, has reached the level of the disciplined, is not terrified or anxious in mind, and is not envious. And when, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not dwell upon any phenomena <note>original: "dharma"</note> but observes the true nature of things as they are. That which is the non-clinging and non-conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the proper conduct of a bodhisattva and mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association for a bodhisattva and mahasattva? 
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not frequent kings, nor does he frequent princes, royal ministers, or royal officers. He does not associate with, serve, or approach them. He does not associate with, serve, or approach followers of other paths <note>original: "anyatirthya"</note> such as wandering mendicants, itinerant monks, members of the <term>Ajivika</term> <gloss>a fatalist sect</gloss> or <term>Nirgrantha</term> <gloss>Jain</gloss> sects, nor those devoted to worldly poetry and secular treatises. He does not associate with, serve, or approach those who maintain worldly or materialistic spells <note>original: "lokayata-mantradharakan"</note>, nor does he form friendships with them. He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, those who strike with fists, pig-breeders, poultry-breeders, 
<margin>N 181</margin>
deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or play belonging to others. He does not form friendships with them. However, when such people come to him, he preaches the Law to them at the appropriate time, but he does so without relying on them <note>original: "anishrita", meaning without expectation of reward or social attachment</note>. 

He does not associate with, serve, or approach monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the vehicle of the Disciples <note>original: "Shravakayana"</note>, nor does he form friendships with them. He does not frequent the same places with them, whether in walking paths or in monasteries. However, when they come to him, he preaches the Law at the appropriate time, and he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the proper sphere of association for a bodhisattva and mahasattva.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, Manjushri, a bodhisattva and mahasattva does not preach the Law repeatedly to women by seizing upon signs of affection for one or another, nor is he desirous of seeing women repeatedly. He does not frequent the households of others, nor does he think he should converse frequently with girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Law to eunuchs, nor does he form friendships or exchange greetings with them. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, except when he is practicing the mindfulness of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Buddha/Thus-Gone One</gloss>. If he does preach the Law to women, he does not preach even the Law with a mind of attachment to the Law <note>let alone with worldly desire</note>.

<summary>The Buddha explains the first of four "Peaceful Practices" for bodhisattvas in the final age, focusing on proper conduct and avoiding distracting or harmful social associations. The passage details specific groups, such as worldly officials, other religious sects, and certain professions, that a practitioner should avoid to maintain spiritual focus.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Peaceful Practices, Bodhisattva, Proper Conduct, Final Age, Lotus Sutra, Tathagatanusmriti</keywords>

->13. The Chapter on the Pleasant Abode<-

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then indeed, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, the Youthful Prince, said this to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, O Blessed One, extremely difficult what has been undertaken by these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <term>Mahāsattvas</term> out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, O Blessed One, should this <term>Dharmaparyāya</term> be proclaimed by these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <term>Mahāsattvas</term> in the future time, in the final age?" When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, the Youthful Prince: "When established in four things, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> should proclaim this <term>Dharmaparyāya</term> in the future time, in the final age. In which four? Here, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, when established in the proper conduct and sphere of action, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> should proclaim this <term>Dharmaparyāya</term> in the future time, in the final age. And how, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, does a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> become established in the proper conduct and sphere of action? When, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> is patient, gentle, has attained the stage of gentleness, is not terrified or agitated in mind, and is not critical; and when, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> does not dwell on any phenomenon, but observes the true nature of phenomena as they are. That which is the non-observation and non-conceptualization of these phenomena, this, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, is called the proper conduct of a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term>. And what, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, is the
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
sphere of action of a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term>? When a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> does not serve kings, nor serve, associate with, attend upon, or approach princes, high ministers of state, or royal officers; nor serve, associate with, or attend upon other sectarians such as wandering mendicants, pilgrims, <term>Ājīvikas</term>, or <term>Nirgranthas</term>, nor beings devoted to poetry and worldly treatises; nor serve, associate with, or attend upon those who hold to the spells of the materialists or the materialists themselves, and does not make friends with them. He does not associate with outcasts, fist-fighters, pig-breeders, poultry-breeders, hunters, 
<margin>N 181</margin>
butchers, actors, dancers, wrestlers, or others. He does not approach places of amusement or sports belonging to others. He does not make friends with them. When they approach him, he teaches them the Law from time to time, and he teaches it without being dependent on them. He does not serve, associate with, or attend upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, nor does he make friends with them. He does not share a sphere of movement with them, whether in a walking path or in a monastery. When they approach him, he teaches them the Law from time to time, and he teaches it without being dependent on them. This, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, is the sphere of action of a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term>.
<margin>K 277</margin>

Furthermore, <term>Mañjuśrī</term>, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Mahāsattva</term> does not repeatedly teach the Law to women by grasping at the signs of affection for one or another of them, nor does he constantly desire the sight of women. He does not approach families, nor does he think that a girl, a maiden, or a daughter-in-law should be spoken to frequently, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not teach the Law to a eunuch, nor does he make friends with him, nor does he exchange greetings. He does not enter a house alone for the purpose of alms, except while practicing <term>Tathāgatānusmṛti</term>. If he should teach the Law to a woman, he does not teach the Law even with an interest in the Law, let alone

---

1 G: Extremely difficult. 2 G: omits "in the future time, in the final age." 3 G: omits "not terrified." 4 K: is attached. 5 G: conduct and non-observation in phenomena. 6 G: serves. 7 K: taking for grasping. 8 G: does not exchange greetings.

<summary>Mañjuśrī asks the Buddha how Bodhisattvas should preach the Lotus Sutra in the future age of decline. The Buddha explains the first of four requirements, focusing on the proper conduct and sphere of action which involves avoiding worldly powers, certain occupations, and improper associations.</summary>
<keywords>Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva, sphere of action, proper conduct, future age, preaching, social avoidance, ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page is from the Sefer ha-Zohar, Parashat Emor (Folio 104). The layout is a single column of Zoharic text, including a section of the 'Ra'aya Meheimna' (The Faithful Shepherd). The script is Rashi script. The text discusses the spiritual significance of 'Ushpizin' (guests), charity to the poor, and the mystical meaning of the creation of man in the divine image.</meta>

## Main Text (Zohar)

דחזות ליה חולקא בעמיא קדישא יתיר בכלא דמהימנותא לקבלא אושפיזין למחדי בהאי עלמא ובעלמא דאתי. ועבד בעי למחדי למסכני מט' בגין דחולקא דאינון אושפיזין דזמין למסכני הוא וההוא דיתיב בכלא דהמהימנותא ומין אושפיזין אלין עלאין אושפיזין מהימנותא ויהיב לון חולקיהון כלהו קיימי קמיה ואמרי:
> **אל תלחם את לחם רע עין וגו'** <note>משלי כג:ו</note>

השתכח דההוא פתורא דתקין דיליה הוא ולאו דקב"ה עליה כתיב:
> **וזרתי פרש על פניכם וגו' פרש חגיכם וגו'** <note>מלאכי ב:ג</note>

אוי ליה לההוא בר נש בשעתא דאינון אושפיזין מהימנותא קיימי מפתורא. ואמר רבי אבא אברהם כל ימוהי הוה קאים בפרשת אורחין לזמנא אושפיזין ולקבלא לון פתורא השתא דאזמנין ליה ולכלהו צדיקייא ולדוד מלכא ולא יהבין לון חולקהון ההוא קשיא מכולא ואקרי:
> **סורו נא מעל אהלי האנשים הרשעים האלה** <note>במדבר טז:כו</note>

וכלהו סלקין ואמרין: <term>יצחק</term> אמר:
> **ובטן רשעים תחסר** <note>משלי יג:כה</note>

<term>יעקב</term> אמר:
> **פתך אכלת תקיאנה** <note>משלי כג:ח</note>

ושאר כל צדיקייא אמרו:
> **כי כל שלחנות מלאו קיא צואה בלי מקום** <note>ישעיהו כח:ח</note>

<term>דוד מלכא</term> אמר והלכות דיכוי דכתיב ויהי כעפרת הימים וינוף יי' את ככל ומתי מחי קא מיירי בגין דדוד סחל לכבל והתעביד ליה אושפיזא ולא בעא ולא זמין ליה ולא יהב ליה חולקא וכחינון עטרה וימין דדוד מלכא דחין עלמא להלן עלוה ההוא בר נש דאטלים ליה כים יתיר מכלא. אמר ר' אלעזר בנ"כ חסידותא לא פטרת עליה דבר נש יתיר אלא במה דיכול דכתיב ליום כהנתת ידו וגו'. ולא לוחא אינוס חכחא והשבע וארוי קדמיתא ומה דישתאר לתן למסכני אף רוחא דכלא דאושפיזין הוא והיהו לאושפיזין ויהי לון קב"ה חלי עמיה ולברכה קרי עליה:
> **אז תתענג על יי' וגו'** <note>ישעיהו נח:יד</note>

ויצחק קארי עליה:
> **כל כלי יוצר עליך לא יצלח** <note>ישעיהו נד:יז</note>

אמר רבי שמעון האי דוד מלכא א"ל בגין דכל זינין דמלכא וקרבין למלכא בידוי דדוד אתפקדו. חכ"ז מאן דחדי גבור בחלקו ורעו וגו' קטן ועיסר כביט וגו' יעקב אמר לו ויבקע בבקר חורך וגו' שאר צדיקייא אמרו וכהך יי' תמיד והשביע וגו'. דוד מלכא אמר כל כלי יוצר עליך לא יצלח דהוא על כל זיני זינין אתפקד וכלה חולקיה דבר נש זכי לכל האי זכחן חולקיהון דצדיקייא בעלמא דין ובעלמא דאתי עליהו כתיב:
> **ועמך כלם צדיקים וגו'** <note>ישעיהו ס:כא</note>

---

### רעיא מהימנא (The Faithful Shepherd)

-> **ולקחתם לכם ביום הראשון וגו'** <- <note>ויקרא כג:מ</note>

**פקודא** דא ליטול לולב כדקא יאות ביומין אלין ויהי נמיכין וזיין ליה וקאי רזא דאוקימנא ולקחתם פדירוס כמה דקב"ה נטיל לון לישראל בהאי זימנא דדינון. אוף הכי ופרש בעיין ליה לקב"ה בחולקהון וחלוסן ביה. ולפ' קדמא דא לולב וזמין דכיה למיסב רזא דיוקנא דאדם וכן למטה. עב'.

הבקרח סמאי לככולי ברחמיו ובדתיו אף עשותיו. כל הבקרח סמיאי דא אדם דקב"ה קארי ליה סמאי דכתי' ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו ועוד דחקרי בבמיה בשעתא דחפיק קשוט וזיחא בעלמא וחקרי אלהים דכתיב אלהים לא תקלל קרא ליה בבמיה דכתיב ויברא אלהים

---

את האדם בצלמו ושפיר קא לוקימנא דכתיב **נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו** בשעתא דזווגא אתמר. וכך הוא כוונא דתרוייהו בנלס ודמות וחדס דדכר ונוקבא נפק ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו. כפכח דסליק מלכא אשכחנא דבשעתא דזווגא השתכח.

<vocab>
אושפיזין, קב"ה, דוד מלכא, מהימנותא, רעיא מהימנא, צלם, דמות, אברהם, יצחק, יעקב, פקודא, לולב
</vocab>

[context] The second “dwell” refers to human beings;
for he who has a portion in the holy land and people sits in the shadow of faith to receive the guests so as to rejoice in this world and the next. He must also gladden the poor, because the portion of those guests whom he invites must go to the poor. And if a man sits in the shadow of faith and invites these guests and does not give them their portion, they all hold aloof from him, saying “Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye” (Prov. 23, 6). That table which he prepares is his own and not God’s. Alas for him when those guests leave his table.
R. Abba further said: ‘Abraham always used to stand at the cross roads to invite guests to his table. Now when a man invites him and all the righteous and King David and does not give them their portion, Abraham rises from the table and exclaims, “Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men” (Num. 16, 26), and all rise and follow him. Isaac says, “The belly of the wicked shall want” (Prov. 13, 26). Jacob says, “The morsel thou hast eaten thou shalt vomit up” (Ibid. 23, 8). The other righteous ones say, “For all tables are full of vomit and uncleanness” (Isa. 28, 8).
David says: [lacuna] In those ten days during which David judges the world, that man is judged who has treated him more ungratefully than Nabal.’
R. Eleazar said: ‘The Torah does not demand of a man more than he can perform, as it says, “Each one man shall give as he is able,’ (Deut. 16, 7). A man should not say, I will first satisfy myself with food and drink, and what is left I shall give to the poor, but the first of everything must be for the guests. And if he gladdens the guests and satisfies them, God rejoices with him and Abraham proclaims over him, “Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord”, etc. (Isa. 58, 14). Isaac proclaims, “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” (Ibid. 54, 17).’ R. Simeon said: ‘This verse is said by King David, because all royal weapons of war have been handed to David. What Isaac says is, “His seed shall be mighty on the earth” (Ps. 112, 2).
Jacob proclaims, “Then shall thy light break forth as the morning” (Isa. 58, 8). The other righteous say, “The Lord shall guide thee continually and satisfy thy soul in dry places” (Ibid. 11). Happy the lot of the man who attains ta all this!’ AND YE SHALL TAKE YOU ON THE FIRST DAY THE FRUIT OF GOODLY TREES.
R. Simeon quoted here the verse: “Every one that is called by my name, for my glory I have created him, I have formed him, yea I have made him” (Isa. 63, 7). ‘ “Every one that is called by my name”: this is man whom God has created in His likeness and whom He calls by His own name when he does truth and justice, as it is written, “Thou shalt not revile the judges” (Elohim, Ex. 22, 28).
“I have formed him, yea I have made him”: as has been explained, the words “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” refer to the time of wedlock, namely, the union of “image” and “likeness”, so that man issued from Male and Female.
In the Book of King Solomon it is written that at the hour of wedded union on earth,
[context] God sends a certain form with the figure of a human being which hovers over the union, and if a man’s eye were capable of such a thing it would see such a form over his head.

For any person who has a portion in the holy people, it is most necessary of all for their faith to receive the <term>Ushpizin</term> <gloss>sacred guests/spiritual visitors</gloss> and to rejoice in this world and in the world to come. A person must make the poor rejoice, for the portion of those guests whom he invites belongs to the poor. One who sits in the wholeness of faith and invites these high, celestial guests—the guests of faith—and gives them their portion <note>by feeding the poor on earth</note>, all of them stand before him and say:
> **Do not eat the bread of one who has an evil eye...** <note>Proverbs 23:6; here used to contrast with the generous person</note>

It turns out that such a table which he prepares is his own, and not the Holy One's, blessed be He, of which it is written:
> **I will spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your festivals...** <note>Malachi 2:3</note>

Woe to that person at the time when those guests of faith rise from the table. Rabbi Abba said: Abraham, all his days, would stand at the crossroads to invite guests and set a table for them. Now that he and all the righteous ones and King David are invited <note>during the festival of Sukkot</note>, and people do not give them their portion <note>by neglecting the poor</note>, it is the most difficult thing of all, and it is called:
> **Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men** <note>Numbers 16:26</note>

And they all ascend and say: <term>Yitzchak</term> <gloss>Isaac</gloss> says:
> **But the belly of the wicked shall want.** <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>

<term>Yaakov</term> <gloss>Jacob</gloss> says:
> **The morsel which you have eaten, you shall vomit up.** <note>Proverbs 23:8</note>

And all the rest of the righteous ones say:
> **For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean.** <note>Isaiah 28:8</note>

<term>David Malka</term> <gloss>King David</gloss> spoke of the laws of being crushed, for it is written that he becomes like the dust of the seas. <unclear>2 lines of corrupted Rashi script regarding David and the guest portion</unclear>. Because David represents the Crown and the right hand <note>referring to the Sefirot</note>, when a person deprives him, it is as if he pushes the whole world away. Rabbi Eleazar said: A person is not exempt from acts of loving-kindness, but must do according to what he can, as it is written "according to the gift of his hand." One should not feel forced; one should eat and be satisfied first, and what remains should be given to the poor. This is the spirit of the guests, and the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells with him, and the blessing is called upon him:
> **Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord...** <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>

And Isaac calls upon him:
> **No weapon that is formed against you shall prosper.** <note>Isaiah 54:17</note>

Rabbi Shimon said: King David said this because all the types of the King and the battles of the King were entrusted into the hands of David. Whoever rejoices in his portion and his will <unclear>small and tithe</unclear>. Jacob said to him: "Then shall your light break forth as the morning." The rest of the righteous said: "And the Lord shall guide you continually, and satisfy your soul." King David said: "No weapon that is formed against you shall prosper," for he is appointed over all types of weapons. And all this is the portion of the person who merits all these merits, the portion of the righteous in this world and the world to come, of whom it is written:
> **Your people also shall be all righteous...** <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

***

### <term>Ra'aya Meheimna</term> <gloss>The Faithful Shepherd</gloss>

-> **And you shall take for yourselves on the first day...** <- <note>Leviticus 23:40</note>

This **commandment** is to take the <term>Lulav</term> <gloss>palm branch</gloss> as is fitting during these days, to be humble and armed with it. This is the secret we have established: "And you shall take" means <term>pederos</term> <gloss>a precious stone/beloved son</gloss>, just as the Holy One, blessed be He, takes Israel at this time of judgment. So too, they should seek the Holy One, blessed be He, in their portion and take refuge in Him. The first command is the Lulav, which is ready to be taken in the secret of the image of Man, and so it is below.

<unclear>3 lines of fragmented text regarding the Creation and the name of God</unclear>. This refers to Adam, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, calls by the name <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God/Judge</gloss>, as it is written: "And God created man in His own image." Furthermore, it is searched out at the hour when truth and radiance go out into the world. It is written "You shall not revile God" <note>Elohim</note>; He called him by His name, as it is written: "And God created

---

man in His own image." And we have well established that it is written, **"Let us make man in our image, after our likeness,"** which was said at the time of the union <note>the mystical union of divine forces</note>. And such is the intention of both, in image and likeness, and the union of male and female came forth: "And God created man in His own image." Just as the King ascends, we find that at the time of the union, He was found.

## Main Text (Zohar)

He who has a portion in the holy people has a greater duty than all others in the matter of faith: to receive the <term>Ushpizin</term> <gloss>divine guests</gloss> and to rejoice in this world and the world to come. A person must cause the poor to rejoice, for the portion of those guests whom he invites belongs to the poor. One who sits in the wholeness of faith and invites these supernal guests, the guests of faith, but does not give them their portion <note>by failing to feed the poor</note>, they all stand over him and say:
> **Do not eat the bread of one who has an evil eye...** <note>Proverbs 23:6</note>

It turns out that the table he prepared is his own and not the Holy One’s, blessed be He. Concerning him it is written:
> **And I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festival sacrifices...** <note>Malachi 2:3</note>

Woe to that person at the time when those guests of faith rise from his table! Rabbi Abba said: Abraham, all his days, would stand at the crossroads to invite guests and prepare a table for them. Now that he and all the righteous ones and King David are invited <note>spiritually during Sukkot</note>, but are not given their portion, it is harder than all else. It is called:
> **Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men...** <note>Numbers 16:26</note>

And they all rise and depart. <term>Isaac</term> <gloss>representing the attribute of Judgment</gloss> says:
> **...but the belly of the wicked shall want.** <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>

<term>Jacob</term> <gloss>representing Truth/Harmony</gloss> says:
> **The morsel which you have eaten, you shall vomit up.** <note>Proverbs 23:8</note>

And all the other righteous ones say:
> **For all tables are full of filthy vomit, so that there is no place clean.** <note>Isaiah 28:8</note>

<term>King David</term> says <note>text here refers to the crushing of the spirit and King David's role as the poor king/Malchut</note>. Because David represents the Assembly of Israel, and he becomes a guest, but the person did not desire him, nor invited him, nor gave him a portion; therefore the Crown and the Right Hand <note>attributes of Malchut and Chesed</note> push that man out of the world. Rabbi Eleazar said: The Holy One does not demand of a person more than he is able, as it is written: "every man shall give as he is able" <note>Deuteronomy 16:17</note>. One should not say "I will eat and satisfy myself first and give what remains to the poor," for the essence of the guests' portion is first. If one gladdens the guests, the Holy One gladdens him and calls him blessed:
> **Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord...** <note>Isaiah 58:14</note>

And Isaac says over him:
> **No weapon formed against you shall prosper.** <note>Isaiah 54:17</note>

Rabbi Shimon said: King David says this because all the weapons of the King and the King's battles were entrusted into David's hands. Jacob says of him: "Then shall your light break forth as the morning" <note>Isaiah 58:8</note>. The rest of the righteous say: "And the Lord shall guide you continually and satisfy your soul" <note>Isaiah 58:11</note>. King David says: "No weapon formed against you shall prosper," for he is appointed over all types of weapons. One who merits this, his portion is with the righteous in this world and the world to come. Concerning them it is written:
> **Thy people also shall be all righteous...** <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

### The Faithful Shepherd (Ra’aya Meheimna)

-> **And you shall take for yourselves on the first day...** <- <note>Leviticus 23:40</note>

This **commandment** is to take the <term>Lulav</term> <gloss>palm branch</gloss> properly during these days. This is the secret of what we have established: "And you shall take" signifies a gift, just as the Holy One takes Israel at this time of judgment. So too should a person seek the Holy One as his portion. First is the Lulav, which is intended to take the secret of the image of Man <note>the Lulav represents the human spine and the Sefirah of Yesod</note>.

<unclear>OCR text here contains several garbled or non-standard abbreviations</unclear> God created Man in His image, as it is written: "And God created man in His own image" <note>Genesis 1:27</note>. And it is written "Elohim <gloss>God</gloss> you shall not curse" <note>Exodus 22:27, often interpreted as referring to judges or divine beings</note>. 

---

...the Man in His image. And it is well-explained as it is written: **"Let us make man in our image, after our likeness"** <note>Genesis 1:26</note>. This was said at the time of the union <note>of the divine attributes</note>. Such is the intention of both: "Image" and "Likeness" refer to the male and female aspects. From their union emerged: "And God created man in His own image."
